Allergen review may be relevant, but should not replace assessment of the full symptom pattern.
takeaway: Assess persistent snoring with disrupted sleep or daytime effects.
learningObjective: Assess persistent snoring with disrupted sleep or daytime effects.

title: A sports concussion return question
stem: A student with a diagnosed concussion has begun light activity under a return plan. Symptoms are improving and the student wants to join a contact game today. What should the nurse reinforce?
options: Full play is reasonable once symptoms feel better at rest
Progress through the return plan and obtain required clearance
A team noncontact practice can be used to test readiness today
Resume contact play once the missed school assignments are finished
why: Improvement at rest does not establish readiness for head-impact risk.
Staged progression and medical clearance for higher-risk stages protect recovery; timing is individualized.
Team practice may carry risk and should match the prescribed stage and clearance requirements, rather than serve as an unscheduled test.
Schoolwork completion alone does not establish physical readiness for contact sport.
takeaway: Reinforce a graduated assessed return after concussion.
learningObjective: Reinforce a graduated assessed return after concussion.

title: Adolescent health goal ownership
stem: A parent requests a diet plan for a teenager who has not yet discussed goals with staff. No urgent nutritional problem has been identified. What should the nurse do first?
options: Review the parent's proposed menu for nutritional balance
Arrange a joint family nutrition teaching session
Invite the teenager to discuss their own priorities and concerns
Record baseline body measurements for the proposed plan
why: Menu review may help after understanding the adolescent's needs and perspective.
Family teaching can be useful, but the teenager should first have a meaningful opportunity to express goals.
A developmentally appropriate discussion establishes the adolescent's perspective before adopting another person's plan.
Measurements do not establish the purpose, relevance or adolescent participation in the proposed change.
takeaway: Include adolescents in defining their own health-promotion goals.
learningObjective: Include adolescents in defining their own health-promotion goals.

title: Preparing for first menstruation
stem: A preadolescent understands the basic explanation of menstruation but worries it may start during class. What teaching best addresses the immediate concern?
options: Review how cycle lengths can vary during adolescence
Explain the reproductive organs using a labelled diagram
Discuss comfort measures for possible menstrual cramps
Plan accessible supplies and a trusted school contact
why: Cycle information is useful but does not provide a response to an unexpected start at school.
The learner already understands the basic process and is asking about practical readiness.
Symptom relief may be discussed, but the immediate concern is managing the first bleeding during class.
Concrete supplies and a person to approach make the expected developmental event more manageable.
takeaway: Pair puberty information with a practical preparedness plan.
learningObjective: Pair puberty information with a practical preparedness plan.

title: Adolescent online health information
stem: A teenager sees an influencer promoting a supplement to improve concentration. Which actions help evaluate the claim? Select all that apply.
options: Check the creator's relevant qualifications
Examine the supporting evidence and when it was updated
Treat the number of likes as evidence of effectiveness
Check whether the creator profits from product sales
why: Relevant expertise helps assess credibility, though it does not by itself prove the claim.
Evidence and currency help distinguish a supported recommendation from a promotional assertion.
Popularity does not demonstrate a clinical benefit or safety.
A financial interest may influence how benefits and limitations are presented.
takeaway: Assess expertise, evidence and commercial influence in online health advice.
learningObjective: Assess expertise, evidence and commercial influence in online health advice.

title: Sexual consent education
stem: During health teaching, a young adult asks whether agreement on a previous occasion means consent today. What is the best explanation?
options: Consent is ongoing and must apply to the current activity
A previous relationship establishes continuing consent
Lack of an objection always establishes consent
Consent is needed only when contraception is not used
why: A prior agreement does not replace voluntary current agreement.
Relationship status does not establish consent for every activity.
Silence or inability to respond does not reliably establish consent.
Consent is separate from contraceptive use.
takeaway: Teach consent as voluntary, specific and ongoing.
learningObjective: Teach consent as voluntary, specific and ongoing.

title: New pain with sexual activity
stem: Eight weeks after birth, a client reports repeated pain during intercourse and worries that a repaired tear has not healed. They have no fever or heavy bleeding. What should the nurse do first?
options: Suggest a lubricant for the next attempt at intercourse
Offer a private assessment of symptoms and healing
Discuss positions that reduce pressure on the perineum
Refer directly for a pelvic-floor exercise program
why: Lubricant may help some causes, but the reported healing concern needs assessment before assuming dryness.
A private review can distinguish healing, tissue, muscle and other contributors and guide appropriate support.
Position changes may improve comfort, but do not clarify the cause of repeated pain or the client's concern about healing.
Pelvic-floor support may be useful after assessing the nature of the discomfort.
takeaway: Invite assessment of postpartum sexual discomfort without assumptions.
learningObjective: Invite assessment of postpartum sexual discomfort without assumptions.

title: Menopause and pregnancy prevention
stem: A 47-year-old who uses condoms has irregular periods and new hot flashes. They do not want pregnancy and ask whether they can stop contraception. What should the nurse recommend?
options: Use cycle tracking as the pregnancy-prevention method
Wait for another menstrual period before using condoms again
Continue pregnancy prevention while reviewing the clinical history
Request one hormone test to decide whether contraception can stop
why: Irregular cycles make prediction difficult and do not establish that pregnancy cannot occur.
Pregnancy can occur before another period confirms continuing ovulation.
Perimenopausal symptoms do not establish loss of fertility; current guidance and individual history should guide stopping.
A single hormone value can fluctuate and does not by itself establish the appropriate stopping point.
takeaway: Do not equate early menopausal symptoms with established infertility.
learningObjective: Do not equate early menopausal symptoms with established infertility.

title: A new changing skin lesion
stem: A client shows photographs of a mole that has become more asymmetric and changed colour over six weeks. It is painless. What should the nurse recommend?
options: Continue photographs until the next annual skin review
Begin a monthly self-check for new itching
Watch for bleeding before arranging a skin appointment
Arrange clinical assessment of the changing lesion
why: Photographs document evolution but do not replace assessment of changes already present.
Itching is not required for a changing lesion to warrant review.
Waiting for bleeding can postpone assessment of concerning evolution.
The documented change warrants clinical evaluation despite the absence of pain.
takeaway: Refer evolving skin lesions rather than waiting for discomfort.
learningObjective: Refer evolving skin lesions rather than waiting for discomfort.

title: Oral health with dry mouth
stem: An older adult has persistent dry mouth after a medication change and reports difficulty eating dry foods. Which approaches are appropriate? Select all that apply.
options: Review possible medication effects with the prescriber or pharmacist
Arrange dental guidance and oral-health prevention
Use frequent sugar-containing lozenges for continuing relief
Assess fluid intake and associated oral symptoms
why: A review can identify modifiable contributors while preserving needed treatment.
Reduced saliva can affect comfort and dental health, so prevention and assessment are useful.
Frequent sugar exposure can increase dental caries risk in an already dry mouth.
Hydration and other symptoms help identify additional causes and the effect on intake.
takeaway: Assess persistent dry mouth and protect oral health while reviewing causes.
learningObjective: Assess persistent dry mouth and protect oral health while reviewing causes.

title: Sun protection with a new medicine
stem: A client starting a prescribed medication with a photosensitivity warning gardens daily. Which plan best reduces exposure while preserving the activity?
options: Use protective clothing and garden during lower-exposure periods
Change to higher-SPF sunscreen for the usual midday session
Take the medicine at bedtime before the next gardening day
Move the garden chair into light tree shade at midday
why: Covering skin and adjusting timing address exposure while retaining the valued activity and prescribed treatment.
Sunscreen helps, but changing SPF alone does not address duration, timing or exposed skin.
Night-time dosing does not necessarily remove the medicine's photosensitizing effect during the day.
Shade can reduce exposure but does not eliminate ultraviolet radiation or the value of other protection.
takeaway: Adapt outdoor routines when medication increases sun sensitivity.
learningObjective: Adapt outdoor routines when medication increases sun sensitivity.

title: Financial strain and nutrition priorities
stem: A client eats ordinary foods comfortably and has no prescribed supplement need. Their remaining food budget could buy a marketed nutrition powder or several days of groceries. What is most useful now?
options: Suggest a trial of the powder at the labelled dose
Plan affordable meals using the available grocery budget
Arrange a routine nutrition referral for next month
Compare the powder's nutrient panel with a standard meal
why: The product has no established individualized indication and may displace the available food budget.
A feasible food plan directly supports the immediate need while further resource support can be explored.
A later review may help but does not address food needs over the next several days.
Product comparison may be informative, but a practical ordinary-food plan directly addresses the immediate budget decision for a client able to eat.
takeaway: Prioritize adequate feasible food access over unassessed commercial products.
learningObjective: Prioritize adequate feasible food access over unassessed commercial products.

title: Movement with a wheelchair
stem: A wheelchair user wants better cardiovascular fitness but develops shoulder pain after five minutes of self-propulsion. An accessible exercise service is available. What should the nurse recommend first?
options: Increase wheelchair-pushing time by five minutes each day
Begin a daily arm-ergometer session at the community gym
Request rehabilitation assessment for an adapted activity plan
Substitute a daily wheelchair sprint for the current routine
why: Increasing load despite pain may aggravate a limitation that has not been assessed.
Arm exercise may be useful, but current shoulder symptoms should inform the chosen modality and intensity.
Assessment can identify a suitable accessible option while accounting for shoulder pain and current endurance.
Higher-intensity propulsion increases shoulder demand and does not address the reported limitation.
takeaway: Make physical-activity plans accessible to current mobility.
learningObjective: Make physical-activity plans accessible to current mobility.

title: Peer education and misinformation
stem: During a class, a participant says they will replace their prescribed treatment with a supplement promoted as a cure. Several others begin writing down the product name. What should the nurse do next?
options: Arrange a private conversation with the participant after class
Ask everyone to review the product website at home
Send the group an evidence resource after the session
Clarify the claim respectfully with the group now
why: Private follow-up may help, but the shared claim is already influencing other participants.
Directing learners to promotional material can reinforce an unexamined claim.
A later resource leaves the immediate potentially consequential misunderstanding unaddressed.
Timely respectful clarification protects learning while avoiding humiliation; individual treatment changes still need appropriate clinical review.
takeaway: Correct health misinformation while preserving participation and respect.
learningObjective: Correct health misinformation while preserving participation and respect.

title: Assessing health-program reach
stem: A free clinic attracts mostly people who already use preventive services. Which changes may improve reach to underserved clients? Select all that apply.
options: Ask nonattenders about access barriers
Partner with trusted local organizations
Use current attendees' preferences to represent nonattenders' needs
Adapt location or hours based on community feedback
why: Nonattender perspectives reveal barriers current users may not face.
Trusted partnerships can improve relevance and access.
Current attendees may not face the barriers that prevent others from using the clinic; their responses alone do not represent the unreached group.
Practical adaptation can address barriers identified by intended users.
takeaway: Evaluate who is missing from a program as well as who attends.
learningObjective: Evaluate who is missing from a program as well as who attends.

title: Newborn jaundice and feeding
stem: During a home visit, a four-day-old newborn is increasingly yellow and unusually difficult to wake for feeds. What is the nurse's priority?
options: Arrange urgent clinical assessment of the newborn
Schedule an additional feeding-support visit tomorrow
Repeat the weight at the next routine home visit
Arrange a routine outpatient bilirubin appointment later in the week
why: Jaundice with abnormal sleepiness and poor feeding can indicate significant illness or bilirubin elevation and requires urgent assessment.
Feeding support is important, but tomorrow's visit would delay assessment of current abnormal alertness.
A weight trend can inform care but is insufficient for this concerning current presentation.
The infant's clinical condition needs urgent review rather than delayed laboratory scheduling.
takeaway: Escalate newborn jaundice associated with poor feeding or unusual sleepiness.
learningObjective: Escalate newborn jaundice associated with poor feeding or unusual sleepiness.

title: Postpartum infection warning
stem: On day five after birth, a client reports a temperature of 38.6°C, increasing pelvic pain and foul-smelling discharge. What should the nurse advise?
options: Review perineal hygiene at the next home visit
Obtain prompt clinical assessment today
Recheck temperature after an antipyretic before deciding
Discuss the discharge at the scheduled postpartum review
why: Hygiene advice does not evaluate a possible postpartum infection.
Fever with increasing pelvic pain and abnormal odour requires prompt assessment for infection and treatment.
A lower temperature after medication would not resolve the infection concern raised by the combined findings.
Routine review is too delayed for the current symptom pattern.
takeaway: Teach prompt assessment for postpartum fever with worsening pain or abnormal discharge.
learningObjective: Teach prompt assessment for postpartum fever with worsening pain or abnormal discharge.

title: Postpartum thrombosis-prevention planning
stem: After an uncomplicated birth, a client prefers staying in bed most of the day despite being cleared for mobilization. Which teaching best supports thrombosis prevention?
options: Resume regular gentle movement according to the recovery plan
Delay routine walking until postpartum bleeding has ended
Substitute seated ankle movements for all permitted walking
Use compression stockings as the entire prevention plan
why: Appropriate mobilization reduces prolonged immobility while respecting recovery.
Expected postpartum bleeding alone does not justify prolonged inactivity after clearance to mobilize.
Ankle exercises may complement care but need not replace tolerated permitted movement.
Mechanical measures, when indicated, complement rather than automatically replace an individualized activity plan.
takeaway: Encourage appropriate postpartum mobility within the individual recovery plan.
learningObjective: Encourage appropriate postpartum mobility within the individual recovery plan.

title: Postpartum bleeding change
stem: A client one week after birth reports suddenly much heavier vaginal bleeding and feels faint while sitting. Which advice takes priority?
options: Call the routine postpartum line and leave a message
Ask a relative to drive to the usual clinic
Rest, drink fluids and measure the next pad
Call emergency services for immediate help
why: A routine callback can delay assessment of possible circulatory compromise.
Family transport to a routine clinic may not provide timely emergency support if the client deteriorates.
Rest can be appropriate while help is coming, but fluids and pad counting do not replace emergency evaluation.
Heavy bleeding with faintness raises concern for significant blood loss requiring emergency assessment and treatment.
takeaway: Treat heavy postpartum bleeding with faintness as an emergency.
learningObjective: Treat heavy postpartum bleeding with faintness as an emergency.

title: Parent learning after discharge
stem: Parents are reviewing when to seek help for their newborn. Which observations need prompt clinical attention? Select all that apply.
options: Unusual difficulty waking enough to complete feeds
Brief hiccups after a feed with comfortable breathing
Persistent chest retractions with difficulty feeding
Occasional sneezing while feeding and activity remain usual
A marked feeding reduction accompanied by fewer wet diapers
why: Abnormal alertness and poor feeding can signal illness or inadequate intake and need prompt assessment.
Brief uncomplicated hiccups are common and do not by themselves indicate urgent illness.
Persistent respiratory distress requires immediate emergency assessment rather than a routine callback.
Isolated sneezing with otherwise normal function does not carry the same urgency as respiratory distress or reduced intake.
A sustained change in feeding and urine output raises concern for inadequate intake or illness.
takeaway: Include feeding, alertness and breathing warning signs in newborn teaching.
learningObjective: Include feeding, alertness and breathing warning signs in newborn teaching.

title: Childhood fever learning focus
stem: A caregiver asks why a child with a lower temperature might need help sooner than one with a higher fever. Which example best demonstrates this?
options: A toddler at 38.1°C is breathing with marked effort
A preschooler at 39.0°C is drinking and playing
A school-age child at 38.5°C asks for a drink
A toddler at 38.8°C settles comfortably with a parent
why: Significant breathing difficulty requires urgent assessment regardless of the modest temperature reading.
The fever still needs monitoring, but normal intake and activity are reassuring compared with respiratory distress.
Requesting and taking fluids is a useful reassuring sign in the absence of other concerning findings.
Comfort and responsiveness matter alongside temperature; this description lacks the urgent breathing cue.
takeaway: Teach assessment of the whole child rather than temperature alone.
learningObjective: Teach assessment of the whole child rather than temperature alone.

title: Preparing a child's hospital visit
stem: A school-age child asks whether a planned blood test will hurt. Which response best prepares the child?
options: Let me show you the equipment before we discuss sensations
You may feel a brief pinch; we can practise your coping plan
Ask your caregiver what happened during their blood test
Look at this game while I get everything ready
why: Equipment demonstration can help but should not postpone answering the direct concern.
An honest concise description paired with agreed coping support provides realistic preparation.
A caregiver's experience may differ and does not replace the nurse's direct explanation to the child.
Distraction can be useful, but preparation should also answer the child's question honestly.
takeaway: Give honest age-appropriate information about expected procedural sensations.
learningObjective: Give honest age-appropriate information about expected procedural sensations.

title: A new caregiving arrangement
stem: A grandparent who will care for an infant plans to use a pillow for sleep; the parents were taught to keep the sleep space clear. The family wants the grandparent involved. What is most useful?
options: Give the parents another copy of the safe-sleep leaflet
Ask the parents to relay the updated advice tonight
Review the sleep setup together and check caregiver understanding
Arrange a separate teaching visit after care has started
why: Another copy for the parents does not establish the grandparent's understanding.
Relayed information can help but may leave the specific difference unresolved.
Shared practical review directly addresses the conflicting plan and supports a consistent routine.
Waiting until care begins leaves the known setup issue unresolved for the first sleep.
takeaway: Update and coordinate health teaching across the infant's caregivers.
learningObjective: Update and coordinate health teaching across the infant's caregivers.

title: Choosing developmentally useful toys
stem: A four-month-old turns toward a parent's voice and reaches for a simple rattle. The parent wonders whether an expensive electronic activity centre is necessary for development. Which activity best builds on the infant's cues?
options: Use recorded speech from a toy during independent play
Provide a new electronic sequence at each play period
Use the activity centre for the main daily play session
Respond to sounds and take turns exploring the safe rattle
why: Recorded speech does not adapt to this infant's signals like responsive interaction.
Novelty alone does not establish a better developmental experience.
An activity centre may be one option, but is not necessary to support the observed interest and interaction.
Responsive turn-taking and safe exploration build on the infant's current social and motor behaviours.
takeaway: Emphasize responsive play over costly developmental marketing.
learningObjective: Emphasize responsive play over costly developmental marketing.

title: Evaluating a prevention plan over time
stem: A client met a regular-meal goal that included dinner at 18:00. They are moving to evening shifts with uninterrupted duties from 17:00 to 20:00 and a meal break at 20:00. A refrigerator is available. Which adaptations are useful? Select all that apply.
options: Review meal times and foods that fit the new break
Prepare meals that can be stored safely at work
Keep the previous meal times for the first month
Arrange a follow-up to review the new routine
why: Planning around actual break availability makes the goal feasible in the changed schedule.
Available storage can support a practical meal strategy matched to the workplace.
The previous 18:00 meal conflicts with the stated period of uninterrupted duties, so retaining that timing does not adapt the plan to the new conditions.
Early review allows the client and nurse to evaluate and refine the adaptation.
takeaway: Reassess and adapt health-promotion plans when circumstances change.
learningObjective: Reassess and adapt health-promotion plans when circumstances change.

title: Clarifying a vague concern
stem: A client awaiting biopsy results says, "I cannot deal with what comes next." What response best clarifies the concern?
options: Which part of what comes next feels hardest right now?
What has your physician explained about the possible results?
Which coping strategy helped during your last health concern?
Would you like to discuss support available after diagnosis?
why: The statement is ambiguous; a focused open question lets the client identify the immediate meaning and concern.
Information already received is relevant but may not reveal what the client means by being unable to cope.
Past coping can be explored after understanding the current difficulty.
Available support may help, but first clarify the particular concern rather than assuming it relates to a diagnosis.
takeaway: Clarify the client's meaning before offering reassurance or solutions.
learningObjective: Clarify the client's meaning before offering reassurance or solutions.

title: Observing inconsistent cues
stem: A client says the upcoming operation is 'fine' while trembling and avoiding discussion. What should the nurse say?
options: 'You should not be frightened.'
'I notice your hands shaking; how are you feeling about tomorrow?'
'Your consent form shows you are comfortable.'
'We can discuss it after surgery.'
why: Telling the client how to feel discourages disclosure.
A neutral observation invites clarification without assuming emotion.
Consent does not establish absence of anxiety.
Delay misses a current opportunity for support.
takeaway: Explore discrepancies between verbal and nonverbal communication.
learningObjective: Explore discrepancies between verbal and nonverbal communication.

title: Responding to anger about waiting
stem: A client says, "No one cares; I have waited all morning." No threats are present, and the nurse does not yet know what help the client needs. What is the best response?
options: The team is working through the morning appointments.
I can check how much longer the wait will be.
This wait sounds frustrating. What help do you need now?
I can explain how to raise concerns with the manager.
why: A queue explanation does not establish whether a current care need has gone unmet.
An estimate may help later, but the immediate need should first be clarified.
Acknowledging the experience and inviting the specific need supports a practical current response.
The complaint process can be offered, but does not replace responding to the present concern.
takeaway: Acknowledge frustration before clarifying what assistance is needed.
learningObjective: Acknowledge frustration before clarifying what assistance is needed.

title: Avoiding premature advice
stem: A capable client is deciding whether to tell an adult child about a diagnosis and asks, "What would you do?" What response best supports the client's decision?
options: I would usually suggest telling a close family member.
Family disclosure often helps people obtain practical support.
Would you like me to ask your child to visit?
What concerns you about telling your child?
why: The nurse's preferred choice may not fit this relationship or the client's priorities.
General benefits may be useful, but the client's specific concern has not yet been explored.
Inviting the child may move toward disclosure before the client has decided what they want.
Exploring the client's concerns supports their own decision about benefits, risks and preferences.
takeaway: Support decision-making without substituting the nurse's personal choice.
learningObjective: Support decision-making without substituting the nurse's personal choice.

title: Checking shared understanding
stem: During a sensitive interview, a client uses an unfamiliar expression and says the nurse's first interpretation was wrong. Which actions help establish the intended meaning? Select all that apply.
options: Use the expression's most common dictionary meaning
Ask the client to explain the expression in their own words
Offer a likely interpretation and begin planning from it
Summarize the clarified meaning and invite correction
why: A common definition may not reflect this client's personal or cultural meaning.
The client's explanation provides direct evidence of the intended meaning.
A plausible guess should not become the basis for planning before the client verifies it.
Checking the revised understanding reduces the chance of carrying the earlier error forward.
takeaway: Verify meaning rather than assuming shared understanding.
learningObjective: Verify meaning rather than assuming shared understanding.

title: A client declines conversation
stem: A client newly diagnosed with cancer says, 'I do not want to talk now.' They show no immediate safety concern. What should the nurse do?
options: Continue questioning to prevent avoidance
Respect the request and agree how to reconnect later
Ask relatives to persuade the client immediately
Document refusal of all psychosocial support
why: Continued pressure can undermine trust.
Respect and a planned return preserve access to support.
Immediate persuasion may disregard the client's expressed boundary.
Declining now does not mean rejecting future support.
takeaway: Respect temporary limits while keeping support available.
learningObjective: Respect temporary limits while keeping support available.

title: Supporting slowed responses
stem: A client with depression pauses for a long time before answering but remains attentive, says they want to continue, and shows no fatigue. What should the nurse do?
options: Offer a written questionnaire to replace the conversation
Invite a support person to help supply the history
Use one clear question and allow time for the answer
Arrange a shorter interview later in the day
why: Writing may help some clients, but the present client is willing and able to engage with a slower pace.
Another person is not needed to replace the client's own account simply because responses are slow.
Patient pacing supports the demonstrated ability to participate without adding pressure.
A later session may be useful for fatigue, which is not the limiting factor described.
takeaway: Adapt interview pace to the client's processing speed.
learningObjective: Adapt interview pace to the client's processing speed.

title: Naming emotion tentatively
stem: After discussing job loss, a client looks away and clenches their hands. Which response best checks emotion without assuming it?
options: 'You seem upset; what is happening for you?'
'You are clearly angry at your employer.'
'At least you have more free time.'
'You should start job searching today.'
why: Tentative observation allows the client to confirm or correct meaning.
A fixed interpretation may mislabel the emotion.
Positive reframing may minimize a painful loss.
Immediate advice bypasses assessment of current needs.
takeaway: Offer tentative observations and invite the client's interpretation.
learningObjective: Offer tentative observations and invite the client's interpretation.

title: Maintaining therapeutic focus
stem: During discussion of a separation, a client asks for details of the nurse's divorce and says, "Then I can do what you did." What is the best response?
options: I can tell you briefly which decision worked best for me.
I can answer your questions about how my divorce ended.
Would a support group help you compare other people's choices?
Our situations may differ. What decision are you facing?
why: The client is seeking a model to copy; personal advice risks displacing their own needs and judgment.
Detailed personal information shifts the therapeutic conversation toward the nurse's experience.
A group may be useful later, but does not first clarify the decision the client is struggling with.
A respectful boundary and return to the client's situation support individualized decision-making.
takeaway: Limit self-disclosure to preserve the therapeutic focus.
learningObjective: Limit self-disclosure to preserve the therapeutic focus.

title: Communicating through an interpreter
stem: During a mental-health interview, which practices support the client's participation? Select all that apply.
options: Address the client directly
Allow extra time for interpretation
Ask a child relative to interpret trauma details
Clarify confidentiality and the interpreter's role
why: Direct engagement maintains the therapeutic relationship.
Interpretation needs time for accuracy and emotional processing.
A child may lack skills and face inappropriate emotional burden.
Role clarity supports trust and informed participation.
takeaway: Use qualified interpretation with clear roles during sensitive interviews.
learningObjective: Use qualified interpretation with clear roles during sensitive interviews.

title: Ending a therapeutic meeting
stem: A client becomes distressed when the nurse abruptly announces the session is over, saying they did not know how much time remained. What change best addresses this in future meetings?
options: Keep the session length consistent across appointments
Give an ending reminder and confirm the next contact
Offer another short session when distress begins
Provide a written session summary at departure
why: Consistent length helps, but the client also needs an understandable transition cue during the meeting.
Advance notice and continuity information allow preparation for the ending that triggered distress.
Extra contact may occasionally be needed, but does not establish predictable closure.
A summary may support recall but arrives after the abrupt ending has already occurred.
takeaway: Prepare clients for endings and clarify the next contact.
learningObjective: Prepare clients for endings and clarify the next contact.

title: A repeated request for reassurance
stem: A client repeatedly asks whether staff are annoyed with them. Reassurance helps briefly, but the nurse does not know what brings the worry back. What is the best next response?
options: Reassure the client again that staff want to help
Guide a brief breathing exercise when worry returns
Ask what happens just before the worry returns
Arrange a regular time for reassurance check-ins
why: Repeating reassurance may relieve distress briefly but has not revealed the recurring trigger.
A coping exercise may help after the nurse understands the pattern and what the client needs.
Exploring the preceding event can identify the concern and guide a more useful response.
Predictable contact may be helpful, but the specific trigger remains unexplored.
takeaway: Explore triggers when reassurance does not provide lasting relief.
learningObjective: Explore triggers when reassurance does not provide lasting relief.

title: Validating without agreeing
stem: A tearful client says, "My sibling cannot visit. They never cared about me." Which response best acknowledges the client's immediate feeling?
options: It sounds painful to feel unsupported today.
Would you like help calling your sibling now?
What reasons might have prevented the visit?
You told me your sibling supported you last month.
why: This names the present hurt without confirming an unassessed judgment about the sibling.
A call may help later, but first responding to the emotion supports feeling understood.
Exploring reasons shifts toward explanation before acknowledging the current distress.
Previous support may offer perspective, but an immediate counterexample can feel dismissive of the present pain.
takeaway: Validate feelings without endorsing unverified conclusions.
learningObjective: Validate feelings without endorsing unverified conclusions.

title: Exploring strengths in crisis
stem: A client overwhelmed by housing problems says, "Nothing I do works." Which question best assesses an existing coping strength?
options: When does the current housing deadline fall?
Which relatives could offer practical assistance?
Which expense is most urgent this week?
What helped you through a previous difficult situation?
why: The deadline clarifies urgency rather than an existing coping skill.
Potential support is relevant, but this question identifies resources rather than a strategy the client has used successfully.
Financial priorities guide practical planning but do not reveal prior effective coping.
Previous successful responses can identify skills and resources the client may use again.
takeaway: Identify previous coping strengths when a client feels powerless.
learningObjective: Identify previous coping strengths when a client feels powerless.

title: Repairing a communication error
stem: Which actions help repair an interview after the nurse realizes a client's statement was misunderstood? Select all that apply.
options: Acknowledge the misunderstanding
Invite clarification of the client's intended meaning
Apologize and move to the next interview topic
Reflect the corrected meaning back to the client
why: Honest acknowledgment can support trust.
The client should establish what they meant.
An apology alone leaves the information error unresolved if the discussion moves on.
Reflection verifies that the revised understanding is accurate.
takeaway: Repair misunderstandings openly and verify the corrected meaning.
learningObjective: Repair misunderstandings openly and verify the corrected meaning.

title: Anxiety before a procedure
stem: A client awaiting a procedure can discuss worries and concentrate, but repeatedly asks what will happen during it. Which intervention best fits the current need?
options: Give a short explanation and check the client's questions
Provide the full written procedure-information leaflet
Begin a relaxation exercise before discussing the procedure
Ask about a prescribed as-needed anxiety medicine
why: The client can engage and is seeking procedural clarity, so focused information directly addresses the uncertainty.
Written information may supplement teaching, but a full leaflet may not answer the specific repeated questions.
Relaxation may help, but should not replace answering the information need when the client can participate.
Medication may be appropriate in some circumstances, but current findings support a focused communication intervention.
takeaway: Match information complexity to the client's ability to process anxiety.
learningObjective: Match information complexity to the client's ability to process anxiety.

title: Unexpected chest symptoms
stem: A client with a history of panic reports new chest pressure and sweating unlike their usual episodes. What should the nurse do first?
options: Compare the sensation with earlier panic episodes
Assess physical status and activate timely clinical evaluation
Coach the breathing technique used for past panic
Offer the prescribed as-needed anxiety medicine
why: History is relevant, but should not delay urgent assessment of new potentially physical symptoms.
A psychiatric diagnosis does not exclude acute physical illness; the changed symptom pattern requires prompt assessment and escalation.
Calm support can accompany assessment, but breathing practice alone would risk attributing the presentation to panic.
An anxiety medicine does not evaluate the new chest symptoms and could delay recognition of illness.
takeaway: Assess new physical symptoms without diagnostic overshadowing.
learningObjective: Assess new physical symptoms without diagnostic overshadowing.

title: After a panic episode
stem: A client's acute panic has settled and concentration has returned. Which next step most directly develops a response to future episodes?
options: Arrange additional reassurance visits with the nurse
Reduce the client's exposure to the immediate stressor
Review early cues and rehearse a chosen coping response
Review whether prescribed medicines were taken consistently
why: Additional contact can support the client, but does not directly practise their own early response.
Temporary stress reduction may help, but does not build a response for unavoidable future anxiety.
With concentration restored, the client can connect early signs with a practised action.
Medication use is relevant, but the stated goal is to develop a practical coping response.
takeaway: Review panic triggers and coping after the client regains focus.
learningObjective: Review panic triggers and coping after the client regains focus.

title: Generalized worry and function
stem: A client with persistent worry has begun missing work. The nurse has reviewed worry themes, duration and physical symptoms. Which further assessment most directly guides support for the new impairment?
options: Effects on daily tasks and coping attempts at work
Relatives' histories of anxiety and treatment
Situations that first triggered worry years ago
The probability of each feared event occurring
why: Current functional effects and attempted responses show where support and treatment goals are needed now.
Family history can inform assessment, but does not describe how the present work difficulty can be addressed.
Historical triggers may be relevant, but current functioning is the newly identified problem.
Testing feared probabilities may be a later therapeutic strategy; it does not establish the practical effect on current roles.
takeaway: Assess how anxiety affects function and what sustains it.
learningObjective: Assess how anxiety affects function and what sustains it.

title: Preparing for graded exposure
stem: A client's agreed phobia plan starts with standing near a closed lift for two minutes using a coping skill. After one minute, the client reports tolerable anxiety and wants to complete the step. What should the nurse do?
options: Offer a short lift ride while the client feels willing
Explain the lift's safety features for the remaining minute
End the practice now because anxiety is still present
Support completion of the current step and review the response
why: Advancing to a different step is not required simply because the client is willing to continue the current one.
Technical reassurance does not replace practising the selected coping response during exposure.
Tolerable anxiety does not necessarily require stopping a collaborative graded exercise.
The client is tolerating and consents to the planned step; completing it provides information for the treatment team's next decision.
takeaway: Support agreed gradual exposure without improvising coercive challenges.
learningObjective: Support agreed gradual exposure without improvising coercive challenges.

title: Anxiety coping skills
stem: A client has manageable anxiety and asks to practise coping between therapy visits. Repeated reassurance calls have provided only brief relief. Which additions support a more independent plan? Select all that apply.
options: Practise noticing present surroundings during rising anxiety
Rehearse a comfortable paced-breathing exercise
Request reassurance from a different person whenever worry returns
Link early warning cues to a chosen coping action
why: Present-focused grounding offers a response the client can practise independently.
A comfortable rehearsed breathing pattern can be used early when distress rises.
Changing the source of repeated reassurance may preserve the same short-lived relief cycle.
Recognizing cues and linking them to action makes the plan usable before anxiety becomes overwhelming.
takeaway: Practise coping skills when the client can engage and learn.
learningObjective: Practise coping skills when the client can engage and learn.

title: Social anxiety and participation
stem: A client wants to join a support group but fears being called on unexpectedly. With the therapist, the client has chosen to observe the first meeting and consider speaking later. Which arrangement best supports this step?
options: Ask the client to introduce themselves at the start
Confirm an observer role with the group facilitator
Arrange an individual session in place of the group
Offer a seat near the door for the first meeting
why: An immediate introduction adds a speaking demand beyond the chosen initial role.
A clear observer agreement makes the planned first participation step predictable.
Individual support may be useful, but substitutes avoidance for the client's chosen group step.
Door access may provide comfort, but leaves the specific fear of being called on unresolved.
takeaway: Support gradual chosen participation for social anxiety.
learningObjective: Support gradual chosen participation for social anxiety.

title: Caffeine and anxiety patterns
stem: A stable client reports evening palpitations after several energy drinks during study sessions. Which history most directly tests this reported association while further assessment proceeds?
options: The usual sleep schedule during examination weeks
Use of prescribed medicines that can affect heart rate
Caffeine amounts and timing relative to each episode
Any personal history of fainting or chest discomfort
why: Sleep is a relevant contributor, but does not directly connect drink exposure to episodes.
Medication history matters, but addresses a different possible contributor.
Exposure timing and quantity help evaluate the stated association; this does not exclude other medical causes.
Associated red flags are important to urgency, but the question asks which history tests the drink-symptom pattern.
takeaway: Assess stimulant exposure when evaluating anxiety-like symptoms.
learningObjective: Assess stimulant exposure when evaluating anxiety-like symptoms.

title: Anxiety versus immediate learning
stem: A highly anxious client cannot repeat a simple discharge instruction after two short explanations and says, "I cannot take this in." Discharge is not urgent. What should the nurse do next?
options: Help settle the anxiety before retrying the essential teaching
Provide the same instruction in a written handout
Invite a support person to listen to another explanation
Repeat the teach-back question in different words
why: The current readiness barrier is intense anxiety; supportive regulation can improve capacity before essential learning is retried.
Written material can supplement learning but may not resolve current inability to process information.
A support person may help later, but the client's present distress still requires attention.
Further questioning may add pressure while the client is unable to attend to the information.
takeaway: Restore readiness when anxiety prevents learning.
learningObjective: Restore readiness when anxiety prevents learning.

title: Evaluating anxiety improvement
stem: A client who avoided shopping chose a goal of completing a short trip using coping skills. Which outcome best demonstrates progress toward that goal?
options: The client reports lower anxiety while resting at home
The client visits with staff giving continuous reassurance
The client shops at a quieter time with a relative doing the tasks
The client completes a brief trip using the practised coping plan
why: Reduced resting anxiety does not establish progress in the avoided activity.
Supported attendance is a step, but does not show the chosen use of the client's own coping skills.
A quieter setting may help, but having someone else perform the task does not demonstrate the selected functional goal.
Completing the valued task with the practised response directly shows the intended functional change.
takeaway: Evaluate anxiety care through improved function and coping.
learningObjective: Evaluate anxiety care through improved function and coping.

title: Reassurance in health anxiety
stem: A client repeatedly seeks the same reassurance after appropriate assessment. Which approach supports a coordinated plan? Select all that apply.
options: Agree on planned review and symptom-reporting boundaries
Explore distress and coping without promising absolute certainty
Offer a new unplanned test every time worry returns
Ensure genuinely new concerning symptoms receive assessment
why: Consistency can reduce fragmented reassurance-seeking while preserving care.
Emotional support does not require impossible guarantees.
Repeated unplanned testing can reinforce the cycle without addressing distress.
A known anxiety pattern must not exclude new clinical evaluation.
takeaway: Balance consistent health-anxiety care with assessment of new symptoms.
learningObjective: Balance consistent health-anxiety care with assessment of new symptoms.

title: Obsessions and compulsions
stem: A client has unwanted contamination thoughts and repeated washing. The nurse has assessed skin condition and immediate safety. To establish a baseline for the goal of reducing daily interference, which question is most useful?
options: What do you fear would happen if you delayed washing?
How much of each day is taken up by washing?
Which cleaning products do you keep at home?
Who usually reassures you when you feel contaminated?
why: The feared consequence informs treatment, but does not quantify the daily time displaced by the ritual.
Time spent establishes a measurable baseline for the stated functional goal.
Products may contribute to skin problems but are less direct measures of daily interference.
Family accommodation matters to the plan, but does not establish how much time washing currently consumes.
takeaway: Assess distress and functional interference from obsessive-compulsive symptoms.
learningObjective: Assess distress and functional interference from obsessive-compulsive symptoms.

title: An interrupted ritual
stem: As part of an agreed therapist-directed plan, a client with obsessive-compulsive disorder delays repeat handwashing for two minutes. After one minute they feel anxious but want to finish the step. What should the nurse do?
options: Reassure the client again that their hands are clean
Suggest trying the two-minute delay at the next visit
Coach the agreed coping strategy through the remaining minute
Offer to check the hands before the timer finishes
why: Repeated reassurance can become part of the ritual and does not support the agreed response-prevention step.
The client is willing and able to continue; postponement does not build on the current tolerated effort.
Support for the agreed manageable step preserves the client's choice and the treatment strategy.
Checking for the client can reinforce reliance on reassurance rather than support tolerating uncertainty.
takeaway: Respond to ritual-related distress through the coordinated treatment plan.
learningObjective: Respond to ritual-related distress through the coordinated treatment plan.

title: Family accommodation of rituals
stem: A client's family repeatedly checks locks at their request. The first agreed treatment step is for relatives to stop completing the first requested recheck while remaining supportive. The client asks, "Please check the door once more." Which family response implements this step?
options: I will stay while you practise the coping exercise we discussed.
I can read the checking list while you check the lock.
I will check it this once before we use the coping exercise.
I can tell you again that I saw you lock the door.
why: Supportive presence with the agreed coping exercise avoids performing or replacing the requested recheck.
Guiding another check can maintain the ritual rather than support tolerating the urge.
Completing the requested first recheck does not implement the agreed reduction step.
Repeated confirmation can become reassurance accommodation rather than the planned coping response.
takeaway: Coordinate family responses that reduce ritual accommodation without abandoning support.
learningObjective: Coordinate family responses that reduce ritual accommodation without abandoning support.

title: Evaluating OCD treatment progress
stem: A client's agreed treatment goal is to leave home independently by 09:00 rather than spend an hour checking appliances. Which follow-up finding most directly shows progress toward that goal?
options: Distress falls from seven to four while checking still takes an hour
The client identifies more triggers but still misses the morning bus
A relative completes the checks and the client leaves at 09:00
The client reduces checking to ten minutes and leaves alone at 09:00
why: Lower distress is useful, but the stated independent functional goal remains unmet.
Insight is useful but has not yet changed the targeted daily interference.
Timeliness has improved through family accommodation rather than the planned independent behaviour.
Reduced ritual time with independent timely departure demonstrates the specific functional improvement.
takeaway: Evaluate obsessive-compulsive care by distress, ritual time and function.
learningObjective: Evaluate obsessive-compulsive care by distress, ritual time and function.

title: Supporting planned response prevention
stem: A client practising therapist-directed response prevention feels anxious after delaying a ritual. Which nursing actions fit the agreed plan? Select all that apply.
options: Stay supportive while the client uses coping skills
Record response and share it with the treatment team
Complete the ritual for the client
Remind the client of the agreed step without coercion
why: Support helps tolerate distress without automatically reinforcing the ritual.
Observations inform adjustment of the coordinated plan.
Staff completion defeats the purpose of response prevention.
Predictable collaborative guidance supports the treatment agreement.
takeaway: Support planned response prevention without completing the compulsion.
learningObjective: Support planned response prevention without completing the compulsion.

title: Compulsive behaviour and skin injury
stem: Repeated handwashing has left a client with painful superficial fissures that are currently bleeding slightly. The client agrees to hand care but remains afraid of contamination. Which action takes priority now?
options: Compare gentler cleansers available for the next wash
Assess and protect the damaged skin using the wound-care plan
Arrange a treatment-team discussion about the washing ritual
Practise a coping statement for the next urge to wash
why: Gentler products may reduce irritation, but do not first assess and protect the current injury.
The active skin injury needs prompt physical care; support for the compulsive behaviour should also continue.
Coordinated treatment is important for preventing recurrence but does not replace care of the present wound.
Coping practice may support treatment, but the bleeding skin requires attention now.
takeaway: Address physical consequences and psychological drivers of compulsive behaviour.
learningObjective: Address physical consequences and psychological drivers of compulsive behaviour.

title: Hoarding and engagement
stem: A client is distressed about discarding possessions. Boxes block the only exit, while collections in the bedroom do not obstruct movement. The client agrees to one small safety change today. Which goal should the nurse negotiate first?
options: Sort a small collection in the bedroom
Arrange valuations for the most important possessions
Clear a usable path to the exit
Schedule a service to clear the whole home
why: A manageable sorting task may build confidence, but it does not address the immediate blocked exit.
Valuation may explore meaning, but leaves the identified evacuation hazard unchanged.
A clear exit addresses the highest immediate risk within the client's agreed limited change.
Whole-home clearance exceeds the small change currently agreed and is not necessary to address the first safety priority.
takeaway: Begin hoarding-related care with collaboration and specific safety priorities.
learningObjective: Begin hoarding-related care with collaboration and specific safety priorities.

title: Unwanted intrusive thoughts
stem: A client is ashamed of recurrent unwanted images of harming someone and says, "They frighten me because I do not want them." The nurse has not yet assessed current safety. Which question is most important now?
options: Do you feel any urge or intention to act on these images?
When did the images first begin to trouble you?
What do you believe having the images means about you?
Who usually helps you cope when the images occur?
why: Direct assessment distinguishes unwanted thoughts from intent or urges and guides further safety assessment; neither risk nor safety should be assumed.
Onset informs the history, but does not establish present intent or control.
Meaning and distress matter to treatment, but current safety needs clarification first.
Support matters to the plan, but does not establish whether the client may act now.
takeaway: Assess intrusive thoughts without equating them automatically with intent.
learningObjective: Assess intrusive thoughts without equating them automatically with intent.

title: Unexpected touch during care
stem: During a nonurgent assessment, a client startles and asks the nurse to stop touching them. The nurse stops. The client says, "I need to know before anyone moves the gown." What should the nurse do next?
options: Explain the medical purpose of the examination again
Offer a chaperone for the remainder of the visit
Offer an appointment on a different day
Agree on notice and permission before moving the gown
why: Purpose may be helpful, but the client has identified unpredictability of contact as the concern.
A chaperone may provide support, but does not by itself address the requested warning and permission.
Rescheduling may be chosen, but the expressed concern may be accommodated during this visit.
An agreed sequence directly restores the specific predictability and choice the client requested.
takeaway: Stop unwanted touch and re-establish choice during trauma-informed care.
learningObjective: Stop unwanted touch and re-establish choice during trauma-informed care.

title: Trauma-informed planning
stem: Which options may help a client who becomes distressed during examinations? Select all that apply.
options: Agree on a stop signal
Explain each step before contact
Require a complete trauma narrative before offering accommodations
Offer choices about positioning or a support person where feasible
why: A stop signal gives the client a clear way to regain control.
Predictability reduces unexpected sensations and actions.
Accommodations do not require detailed disclosure of trauma.
Feasible choices can increase safety and participation.
takeaway: Offer predictability and choice without requiring trauma disclosure.
learningObjective: Offer predictability and choice without requiring trauma disclosure.

title: Grounding during a flashback
stem: A client crouches behind a chair and says they are back at a past assault scene. No current threat is present. They respond when the nurse says their name and can follow one short cue. Which response is best now?
options: Ask which part of the earlier event has returned
Name the current room and invite noticing the floor beneath their feet
Offer to call a support person to discuss the episode
Suggest moving together to a different room in the clinic
why: Discussing the trauma content can increase focus on the recalled event rather than the present surroundings.
A simple present-focused cue fits the client's current ability to engage and can support grounding.
A support person may help later, but contact is less direct than an available grounding response now.
Changing location may help some clients but adds movement before orientation to the current safe setting.
takeaway: Use calm present-focused grounding during trauma re-experiencing.
learningObjective: Use calm present-focused grounding during trauma re-experiencing.

title: Nightmares and daytime function
stem: A trauma survivor reports nightmares and missed morning appointments. Immediate safety has been assessed, and the client wants help attending treatment. Which assessment most directly guides this goal?
options: The timing and content of the original traumatic event
The names and doses of previously prescribed medicines
The effect of poor sleep on waking, travel and daytime tasks
The relatives available for occasional evening telephone contact
why: Trauma history may be relevant if the client wishes, but detailed event content is not required to identify the current attendance barrier.
Past treatment can inform review, but does not directly explain how the present sleep problem affects attending.
Linking sleep impairment to the practical morning routine identifies where support or treatment adaptation may help.
Support is useful, but evening contact may not address the actual morning obstacle.
takeaway: Assess the functional and safety effects of trauma-related sleep disturbance.
learningObjective: Assess the functional and safety effects of trauma-related sleep disturbance.

title: Disclosure without pressure
stem: A client hints at past violence but says they cannot discuss details. What response best supports care?
options: We can discuss what helps you feel safe without requiring details.
We should complete the full history before deciding what support fits.
We can ask your partner to explain the parts you cannot discuss.
We should pause every assessment topic until you can tell the full story.
why: Safety supports and accommodations do not require a detailed trauma narrative.
Requiring full disclosure before support can undermine control and trust.
Seeking a partner's account may compromise privacy or safety.
Relevant care can continue with sensitive pacing and the client's consent.
takeaway: Support current safety needs without forcing trauma narration.
learningObjective: Support current safety needs without forcing trauma narration.

title: A trauma trigger in the environment
stem: A client requests a partly open door during a sensitive conversation. The room opens onto a busy corridor, but a private room with a screened doorway is available. Which proposal best preserves the client's preference and confidentiality?
options: Keep the current door partly open and speak more quietly
Close the current door and explain the privacy requirement
Offer a support person while using the current closed room
Offer the private room with its doorway partly open
why: Lower volume does not reliably prevent corridor conversations being overheard.
The explanation addresses privacy but does not accommodate the expressed door preference when a feasible option exists.
A support person may help, but the proposed door arrangement remains different from the client's request.
The available private arrangement can preserve both the requested opening and confidentiality, subject to the client's agreement.
takeaway: Accommodate safe environmental preferences that reduce trauma-related distress.
learningObjective: Accommodate safe environmental preferences that reduce trauma-related distress.

title: Avoiding retraumatization
stem: Which nursing practices reduce the risk of retraumatization? Select all that apply.
options: Explain the purpose of sensitive questions
Ask permission before physical contact
Use surprise to prevent anticipatory anxiety
Maintain predictable communication about changes
why: Knowing the purpose supports informed participation.
Permission supports bodily autonomy and control.
Unexpected actions may recreate loss of control.
Predictability reduces uncertainty and supports trust.
takeaway: Use consent and predictable communication throughout trauma-informed care.
learningObjective: Use consent and predictable communication throughout trauma-informed care.

title: Dissociation during an interview
stem: During trauma discussion, a client becomes distant and says the room feels unreal. They remain responsive and previously chose naming objects in the room as a grounding strategy. What should the nurse do first?
options: Repeat the last question using simpler wording
Pause and invite the client to name a nearby object
Offer a quiet interval alone before resuming
Change the interview topic to daily activities
why: Rephrasing continues the interview demand before addressing the altered sense of the present.
Pausing and using the agreed simple cue directly supports reorientation; assess safety and possible medical causes if the presentation warrants.
Quiet may help, but leaving alone does not provide the grounding support the client already selected.
A less sensitive topic may help later, but first address the current disconnection.
takeaway: Pause trauma exploration when dissociation interferes with engagement.
learningObjective: Pause trauma exploration when dissociation interferes with engagement.

title: Recovery after a frightening event
stem: After witnessing a collision, a client has been medically assessed and is safe. They are shaken, have no transport and want to contact a sibling but their phone is damaged. What is the most useful initial offer?
options: Arrange a future appointment for trauma-symptom screening
Provide information about formal trauma-focused therapy
Help contact the sibling and arrange a safe way home
Invite a detailed discussion of the collision before departure
why: Follow-up can be useful but does not address the immediate practical barrier.
Therapy may become appropriate if symptoms persist or warrant it, but the current request concerns support and transport.
Practical help matched to the client's expressed need supports immediate stability and connection.
Detailed retelling is not required to receive support and may not be what the client wants now.
takeaway: Provide needs-based support after trauma without forcing detailed retelling.
learningObjective: Provide needs-based support after trauma without forcing detailed retelling.

title: Trauma care and client control
stem: For a nonurgent intimate examination, a client requests a woman examiner and says they would feel able to proceed with that arrangement. An appropriate woman clinician is available later in the same visit. What should the nurse offer?
options: Coordinate the available woman examiner with the client
Arrange a chaperone for the currently assigned examiner
Explain the current examiner's experience with the procedure
Suggest returning to the clinic on another day
why: The feasible arrangement directly matches the preference that the client says would permit care.
A chaperone may be useful but does not substitute for the expressed examiner preference.
Credentials address competence rather than the particular arrangement affecting this client's sense of safety.
A later date may be chosen, but is not necessary when a suitable agreed alternative is available today.
takeaway: Seek feasible examination arrangements that support client control.
learningObjective: Seek feasible examination arrangements that support client control.

title: Evaluating trauma-informed care
stem: The nurse changes an examination plan to strengthen predictability and the client's control. Which statement most directly shows those aims were met?
options: I can name two breathing methods that help me settle.
I understand why this examination was recommended.
I plan to return even though I still feel nervous.
I know the next steps and how to ask for a pause.
why: Coping skills are useful, but this statement does not demonstrate knowledge of the sequence or control over pausing.
Understanding the purpose supports consent, but is different from predicting the process and directing a pause.
Willingness to return is encouraging, but does not establish the two specific aims.
Knowing the sequence and the available stop signal directly demonstrates predictability and agency.
takeaway: Evaluate trauma-informed care through perceived safety, predictability and control.
learningObjective: Evaluate trauma-informed care through perceived safety, predictability and control.

title: Supporting a trusted companion
stem: A trauma survivor wants a friend present during education but not during examination. Which actions are appropriate? Select all that apply.
options: Clarify the client's desired boundaries
Arrange the companion's involvement accordingly
Assume permission for teaching includes permission for examination
Recheck preferences if circumstances change
why: Specific boundaries clarify meaningful consent for involvement.
Respecting the distinction supports control and privacy.
Consent for one context does not automatically extend to another.
Preferences may change and should remain open to review.
takeaway: Treat support-person involvement as specific and revisable.
learningObjective: Treat support-person involvement as specific and revisable.

title: Depression hidden by physical complaints
stem: An older adult has three weeks of fatigue and poor concentration. Medication and medical reviews are underway. They deny feeling sad but say they have stopped gardening, which they used to enjoy. Which question best explores a possible depressive symptom?
options: Has the new medication changed how you sleep at night?
Do activities you usually enjoy still give you pleasure?
Who can help with gardening while your energy is low?
How many hours of sleep do you get on most nights?
why: Medication and sleep effects deserve assessment but do not directly explore the loss of pleasure suggested here.
Loss of pleasure can occur even when a client does not identify sadness; this question explores that cue in accessible language.
Practical help may support function but does not clarify why the valued activity stopped.
Sleep is relevant, but the specific new cue is reduced engagement in a previously enjoyable activity.
takeaway: Assess depression through function and interest as well as reported sadness.
learningObjective: Assess depression through function and interest as well as reported sadness.

title: Small tasks during severe depression
stem: A client with depression wants to resume showering and can physically perform the task, but says starting feels overwhelming. Which plan best supports the agreed self-care goal?
options: Complete the shower for the client this morning
Defer showering until the client feels more motivated
Agree on the first step and provide graded prompting
Substitute a full assisted bed bath for the planned shower
why: Completing the task for the client meets hygiene needs but provides less practice in the desired independent function.
Waiting for motivation can prolong inactivity when a small supported start is feasible.
A manageable first step with support targets initiation while preserving participation in the chosen task.
A less demanding wash may be useful if needed, but the client wants and can attempt the shower with support.
takeaway: Support depressed clients with manageable activities and graded assistance.
learningObjective: Support depressed clients with manageable activities and graded assistance.

title: Responding to worthlessness
stem: A client with depression says, "I am useless because I cannot work." Which reply best explores the meaning of that belief before problem-solving?
options: Work seems closely tied to your sense of worth; what does it mean to you?
You still contribute to your family; shall we list those contributions together?
Would a social worker help you explore financial support while you recover?
Which parts of your old job might you feel able to do now?
why: Reflection followed by an open question invites the client's understanding rather than assuming the problem to solve.
Identifying strengths can be useful, but begins reframing before understanding the belief.
Financial support may be relevant, but the statement concerns worth and its personal meaning.
Capacity assessment may help planning, but does not first explore the connection between work and self-worth.
takeaway: Explore self-worth beliefs without relying on contradiction or comparison.
learningObjective: Explore self-worth beliefs without relying on contradiction or comparison.

title: Behavioural activation planning
stem: A client with depression values tending plants but has stopped. They can tolerate brief activity and agree to try five minutes after breakfast. Which plan best applies this goal?
options: Read a gardening article after breakfast
Watch a gardening programme during the morning
Attend an hour-long community gardening group
Water one plant and review the experience afterward
why: Reading may be enjoyable but does not practise the chosen hands-on activity.
Viewing can provide interest but is less direct than the agreed active step.
A full group session exceeds the brief starting duration the client currently agrees to.
A short valued action matches the goal and permits evaluation of how manageable and meaningful it felt.
takeaway: Use brief personally meaningful activities in a coordinated depression plan.
learningObjective: Use brief personally meaningful activities in a coordinated depression plan.

title: Assessing depressive impairment
stem: Which findings contribute to assessment of a possible depressive episode? Select all that apply.
options: Loss of pleasure in previously valued activities
Sustained changes in sleep and daily function
One isolated preference for quiet time
Persistent feelings of worthlessness
why: Loss of interest is a relevant depressive symptom.
Sustained changes help establish impact and pattern.
A single preference does not establish a depressive syndrome.
Worthlessness warrants further mood and safety assessment.
takeaway: Assess sustained symptom patterns and functional impact in depression.
learningObjective: Assess sustained symptom patterns and functional impact in depression.

title: Depression and decision load
stem: A client with depression is hungry and alert but becomes distressed while comparing six breakfast choices, saying, "I cannot sort them out." What should the nurse try?
options: Give the six-item menu in writing to compare
Offer two acceptable choices and time to respond
Ask a support person to select the usual breakfast
Return after a short break with the same menu
why: Written information may help memory, but the main difficulty is the number of decisions to compare.
Reducing choice burden supports participation while retaining the client's decision.
A familiar choice may help intake but bypasses an opportunity to support the client's own decision.
A break may help fatigue, but the client is alert and the number of choices remains unchanged.
takeaway: Reduce decision complexity while preserving choice during depression.
learningObjective: Reduce decision complexity while preserving choice during depression.

title: Family interpretation of depression
stem: A spouse says, "If they cared about us, they would get out of bed." The client with depression wants to take part in one morning activity but struggles to begin. Which reply best supports the family?
options: You could take over the morning tasks until their energy returns.
A fixed daily target may help; remind them of family responsibilities.
Depression can impair starting tasks; let us plan one supported step.
Make a chart showing how much each family member completes daily.
why: Taking over may ease immediate demands but can reduce opportunities for the participation the client wants.
A target may help, but responsibility reminders can reinforce blame when initiation is impaired.
Explanation reduces moral judgment and a manageable supported step fits the client's expressed goal.
Comparative tracking can intensify blame and does not address how to support the specific initiation difficulty.
takeaway: Explain depressive impairment without removing all expectations for supported activity.
learningObjective: Explain depressive impairment without removing all expectations for supported activity.

title: Evaluating depression recovery
stem: A client recovering from depression chose preparing a simple breakfast independently as a goal. Which one-week outcome most directly demonstrates progress?
options: Prepared breakfast on five mornings with fewer prompts
Explained how mood can affect daily routines more clearly
Selected breakfast each day after staff narrowed the choices
Reported a better mood during two afternoon visits
why: Repeated performance with less assistance demonstrates progress toward the stated independent task.
Understanding is useful, but does not demonstrate the targeted daily function.
Decision support may be progress in another area, but does not establish independent breakfast preparation.
Improved mood matters, but does not directly show achievement of this functional goal.
takeaway: Evaluate depression using sustained function and symptom patterns.
learningObjective: Evaluate depression using sustained function and symptom patterns.

title: Depression screening result
stem: A client has an elevated depression screening score but has not had a diagnostic assessment. Which explanation is accurate?
options: The score establishes depression when the symptoms feel severe.
The score identifies which treatment should be started first.
The score needs a second identical result to establish depression.
The score identifies symptoms needing clinical and safety assessment.
why: A screening score does not by itself establish a clinical diagnosis.
Treatment decisions also require clinical assessment, history, preferences and safety considerations.
Repeating the screening is not a substitute for diagnostic assessment.
Screening identifies concern and helps guide further assessment; it does not complete that assessment.
takeaway: Use depression screening as a route to clinical assessment.
learningObjective: Use depression screening as a route to clinical assessment.

title: Supporting depression follow-up
stem: Which discharge preparations support continuity for a client recovering from depression? Select all that apply.
options: Confirm a follow-up appointment and an access plan
Review early worsening signs and whom to contact
Ask the client to arrange follow-up when symptoms return
Identify practical support for agreed daily routines
why: A confirmed feasible appointment supports planned continuity after discharge.
Recognizing change and knowing an accessible response make the plan usable.
Waiting for recurrence to arrange care can delay support; proactive follow-up remains useful during recovery.
Practical help can support participation in meaningful routines after leaving care.
takeaway: Plan depression follow-up around access, recurrence signs and daily supports.
learningObjective: Plan depression follow-up around access, recurrence signs and daily supports.

title: Postpartum mood assessment
stem: At six weeks postpartum, a client reports persistent hopelessness, poor functioning and inability to enjoy anything. Which plan is most appropriate now?
options: Arrange respite support and review mood at the next routine visit
Arrange timely mental-health assessment and assess immediate safety
Provide a sleep-support plan and review after several better nights
Provide adjustment education and a postpartum peer-group contact
why: Respite may help, but persistent impairment and hopelessness require assessment rather than postponement to routine follow-up.
The sustained symptoms warrant assessment for a perinatal mental-health problem and any immediate safety needs.
Sleep support is useful, but improved rest cannot be assumed to resolve the full symptom pattern.
Education and peer support may complement care but do not evaluate the current significant symptoms.
takeaway: Assess persistent postpartum mood symptoms that impair functioning.
learningObjective: Assess persistent postpartum mood symptoms that impair functioning.
