title: Postpartum psychosis warning
stem: A client one week postpartum has barely slept and believes the infant is controlled by a dangerous force. What is the priority?
options: Arrange supported sleep and reassess the belief after resting
Book a counselling appointment later in the same week
Arrange emergency assessment and supervised parent-infant safety
Complete routine postpartum-depression screening at the next visit
why: Rest is important, but a new delusional belief requires urgent assessment and safety support rather than waiting for sleep.
A later outpatient appointment is insufficient for possible postpartum psychosis and associated immediate risk.
Severe sleep loss and the delusional belief raise an emergency concern; maintain immediate safety while arranging urgent care.
Routine depression screening does not address the urgency or characterize the psychotic presentation.
takeaway: Treat new postpartum psychosis as an emergency.
learningObjective: Treat new postpartum psychosis as an emergency.

title: Adolescent irritability and withdrawal
stem: A teenager has been persistently irritable, withdrawn and less successful at school for a month. A parent has described the change, but the nurse has not yet spoken with the teenager privately. Which next step is most useful?
options: Invite a private discussion of mood, functioning and current safety
Ask the parent to describe the teenager's usual study routine
Review school assignments to identify the most difficult subject
Arrange a joint family meeting about homework expectations
why: The teenager's own account is needed to explore depression, stress, substance use and safety; explain confidentiality and its limits.
The parent's view helps, but has already supplied collateral change and cannot replace the teenager's perspective.
Learning demands may contribute but are only one part of a broader sustained change.
Family planning may help later; expectations alone do not assess the underlying change or immediate concerns.
takeaway: Include depression in assessment of sustained adolescent irritability and decline.
learningObjective: Include depression in assessment of sustained adolescent irritability and decline.

title: Depression with physical illness
stem: After a stroke, a client stops the agreed short rehabilitation sessions and says, "There is no point; nothing will matter again." Pain is controlled and the therapist has confirmed the workload is tolerable. What should the nurse explore next?
options: Whether afternoon sessions would be more convenient
Whether a different analgesic would improve participation
Whether the session should be shortened to two minutes
What the loss of hope means and how mood is affecting participation
why: Timing may influence attendance, but the expressed barrier is loss of hope rather than an inconvenient schedule.
Pain has been assessed and controlled; another analgesic change does not directly address the stated concern.
The workload is tolerable, so reducing it does not clarify the meaning or mood-related barrier.
The statement warrants exploration of mood and meaning, including safety concerns as indicated, while retaining realistic rehabilitation goals.
takeaway: Assess mood when hopelessness interferes with physical rehabilitation.
learningObjective: Assess mood when hopelessness interferes with physical rehabilitation.

title: Monitoring change during treatment
stem: Which changes during depression treatment require prompt reassessment? Select all that apply.
options: New agitation with suicidal thoughts
Markedly reduced need for sleep with unusual impulsivity
A gradual return to a valued routine
New inability to meet basic intake needs
why: Agitation with suicidality can increase immediate risk.
A possible mood switch needs timely clinical review.
Gradual functional improvement is an expected positive outcome.
Inadequate intake can create urgent physical consequences.
takeaway: Reassess new risk, activation or physical compromise during mood treatment.
learningObjective: Reassess new risk, activation or physical compromise during mood treatment.

title: Sudden calm after suicidal distress
stem: A client recently reported intense suicidal thoughts. Today they appear unexpectedly calm after giving away valued possessions. They remain under current protective observation. What should the nurse do next?
options: Update the discharge safety plan to reflect the calmer presentation
Maintain observation and promptly reassess current suicide risk
Ask which possessions were given away and who received them
Encourage a supportive family visit during the afternoon
why: Planning discharge before reassessing the concerning change can misinterpret apparent calm as reduced risk.
The change and possible preparatory behaviour warrant direct current-risk assessment before any reduction in protection.
The details can inform assessment, but should be linked immediately to intent and safety rather than treated as a belongings issue.
Connection may help but does not establish the meaning of the sudden change.
takeaway: Reassess suicide risk when behaviour changes despite apparent mood improvement.
learningObjective: Reassess suicide risk when behaviour changes despite apparent mood improvement.

title: A negative answer with concerning collateral
stem: A client denies suicidal thoughts, but a family member reports farewell messages sent last night. Current observation remains in place. Which next action best clarifies the conflicting information?
options: Repeat the same screening form using its usual wording
Ask the family whether they could supervise at home tonight
Ask the client directly about the messages and current intent
Ask permission to add relatives to the future support plan
why: A standard tool may help but does not replace exploring the specific recent behaviour.
Home support may affect a later plan, but disposition should follow clarification of current risk.
A direct nonjudgmental discussion integrates the collateral report with the client's account and guides further safety assessment.
Support preferences matter, but do not first resolve the immediate discrepancy.
takeaway: Integrate collateral information into suicide-risk assessment.
learningObjective: Integrate collateral information into suicide-risk assessment.

title: Limits of a safety promise
stem: A client under suicide precautions says, "I promise I will not hurt myself." Which plan is appropriate after acknowledging the statement?
options: Continue direct risk assessment and the current prescribed precautions
Replace the current observation with scheduled hourly check-ins
Document the promise as the basis for discharge readiness
Contact the chosen support person and reassess risk afterward
why: The promise is part of the conversation but does not establish safety or replace the assessed protective plan.
Observation changes require appropriate assessment and authorization, not the promise alone.
A promise does not provide sufficient evidence for discharge readiness.
Support involvement is useful, but should not defer the nurse's current risk assessment.
takeaway: Do not use a no-harm promise as a substitute for suicide assessment.
learningObjective: Do not use a no-harm promise as a substitute for suicide assessment.

title: Meaningful protective factors
stem: A client describes an active suicide plan but says responsibility for a pet helps them resist. A friend is available to care for the pet if urgent treatment is needed. What should the nurse do next?
options: Ask the friend to arrange pet care before continuing the interview
Begin a plan for a daily pet-care routine at home
Rate the current risk as low because the client wants to protect the pet
Ask directly about present intent and access to the planned means
why: Pet care can remove a treatment barrier, but should not delay assessment of current danger.
The routine may be protective, but an active plan requires clarification now.
A protective connection does not cancel the risk indicated by an active plan.
Intent and access help determine immediate protection; the pet connection and available help can then be incorporated into care.
takeaway: Assess protective factors without treating them as guarantees against suicide.
learningObjective: Assess protective factors without treating them as guarantees against suicide.

title: Elements of a safety plan
stem: Which components belong in a collaborative suicide safety plan? Select all that apply.
options: Personal warning signs and coping actions
People and services the client can contact
A signed no-harm agreement as the protective strategy
Steps to reduce access to means of self-harm
why: Personal patterns help the client recognize when to begin the plan.
Accessible contacts provide escalating routes for help.
An agreement does not provide the concrete coping, contact and means-safety actions needed during distress.
Practical access reduction can decrease opportunities for harm and should fit the individual situation.
takeaway: Build a practical safety plan with warning signs, coping, contacts and means safety.
learningObjective: Build a practical safety plan with warning signs, coping, contacts and means safety.

title: Practising a crisis plan
stem: A client can name and reach their safety-plan contacts but says, "When distressed, I would not know how to start the conversation." What should the nurse do?
options: Copy the existing contacts onto a wallet card
Rehearse a brief opening request for help together
Ask a support person to make the calls for the client
Add another telephone service to the contact list
why: A portable list helps recall, but the client already knows how to reach the contacts.
Rehearsal directly addresses the stated barrier to initiating help-seeking.
Assistance may be useful if requested, but practising the client's own opening supports the desired independent contact.
More contacts do not by themselves help the client begin speaking during distress.
takeaway: Practise how to request help as part of safety planning.
learningObjective: Practise how to request help as part of safety planning.

title: Confidentiality and acute risk
stem: A client discloses an imminent self-harm plan and asks for secrecy. The nurse's applicable policy requires immediate care-team involvement for serious safety risk. Which explanation is best?
options: I will ask your permission again before I alert the team.
I will begin by asking your family what they think should happen.
I need to involve the immediate care team to help keep you safe.
I will discuss information sharing after the formal assessment is complete.
why: The nurse should explain and involve the client where possible, but the stated urgent duty cannot depend on obtaining permission.
A family opinion does not replace the immediate professional response required by the situation and policy.
A clear explanation identifies the necessary safety disclosure; share relevant information with those who need it under applicable rules.
Postponing the explanation and response leaves an imminent concern unaddressed.
takeaway: Explain necessary safety-related sharing without promising absolute secrecy.
learningObjective: Explain necessary safety-related sharing without promising absolute secrecy.

title: Supervision during an urgent assessment
stem: A client requires prescribed continuous observation for acute suicide risk during transfer. The current trained observer can accompany the client. Which handoff arrangement maintains continuity?
options: The observer stays until a named trained receiving observer accepts responsibility
The transporter supervises while both nurses complete the written handoff
The receiving nurse accepts the chart before finishing another client's care
The current observer leaves after the client enters the receiving assessment room
why: Explicit person-to-person transfer of the observation role preserves the prescribed protection throughout the transition.
Transport accompaniment does not itself establish that the continuous observation role has been accepted by an appropriate observer.
Chart acceptance does not ensure that someone is actively maintaining the prescribed observation.
Arrival in a room does not transfer responsibility unless the receiving observation arrangement is established.
takeaway: Maintain suicide precautions across transitions until appropriately reassessed.
learningObjective: Maintain suicide precautions across transitions until appropriately reassessed.

title: Asking about access to means
stem: During collaborative means-safety planning, a client and chosen support person propose keeping potentially harmful medication in a lockbox. What question most directly checks whether the arrangement will restrict the client's access during a crisis?
options: Will the medication bottles keep their original labels?
Which room will hold the medication box?
When is the next prescription refill due?
Who will control the key or access code?
why: Labels support correct medication use but do not establish restricted access.
Location matters to a practical plan, but a locked box remains accessible if the client controls its opening.
Refill timing may affect supply, but does not determine access to the medication already stored.
Key or code control determines whether the proposed barrier actually limits access; medication delivery needs an agreed safe care plan.
takeaway: Assess access to means to guide concrete protective actions.
learningObjective: Assess access to means to guide concrete protective actions.

title: Evaluating a proposed discharge safety plan
stem: Which findings indicate that a safety plan needs revision before it can be relied upon? Select all that apply.
options: The only listed contact is unreachable overnight
The client cannot access the promised follow-up service
The client identifies a personal early warning sign
The plan relies on evening check-ins, but the support person expects to provide appointment rides
why: An unavailable contact creates a predictable access gap.
A plan depending on inaccessible care is not operational.
Recognizing a warning sign supports plan usefulness.
The mismatch leaves a planned safety function uncovered and should be clarified with everyone involved.
takeaway: Verify that safety-plan resources are reachable and understood.
learningObjective: Verify that safety-plan resources are reachable and understood.

title: Self-injury without stated suicidal intent
stem: A client reports cutting to relieve distress and denies wanting to die. Superficial wounds have been assessed and treated. The nurse has not yet explored current suicidal thoughts or intent. Which action is needed next?
options: Ask directly about current suicidal thoughts, intent and access
Review the agreed dressing-change schedule with the client
Ask which coping activity helped before earlier episodes
Arrange routine follow-up focused on reducing self-injury
why: The stated function of cutting does not establish absence of suicide risk; direct assessment is still needed.
Wound teaching matters, but physical care is already addressed and the current safety assessment remains incomplete.
Coping history is useful, but does not determine whether there is current suicidal intent.
Follow-up planning should be informed by current risk rather than precede its clarification.
takeaway: Assess both physical injury and suicide risk after self-injury.
learningObjective: Assess both physical injury and suicide risk after self-injury.

title: Responding after self-injury disclosure
stem: After wounds are assessed, a client says, "You must think I am attention-seeking." Which reply best opens exploration of the distress associated with the episode?
options: The staff are here to help, and we do not judge you.
What was happening and how were you feeling just before this?
We can review some coping strategies that may help next time.
Would you like me to contact someone you trust for support?
why: Reassurance may help rapport, but does not invite the client's account of the episode.
An open question explores the experience and context without assigning a motive.
Education may follow, but the relevant coping needs should be understood first.
Support contact may be useful, but does not directly explore the distress the client is trying to communicate.
takeaway: Respond to self-injury with nonjudgmental assessment of distress and safety.
learningObjective: Respond to self-injury with nonjudgmental assessment of distress and safety.

title: Choosing safer coping alternatives
stem: A client identifies muscle tension as an early sign before self-injury. They chose a brief noninjurious grounding exercise in the treatment plan and want to practise using it sooner. Which plan best fits that aim?
options: Practise the exercise after wound care when another episode occurs
Replace the exercise with a new strategy at the next visit
Rehearse the exercise when the first muscle tension appears
Request staff reassurance once tension reaches its highest level
why: Post-episode practice may aid learning, but does not move use earlier in the escalation sequence.
A new method may be considered if needed, but the client has already selected one and wants help with timing.
Linking the agreed skill to the identified early cue directly addresses the desired change.
Reassurance may provide support, but waiting for peak tension misses the planned early opportunity.
takeaway: Connect early self-harm cues with rehearsed noninjurious coping.
learningObjective: Connect early self-harm cues with rehearsed noninjurious coping.

title: Digital messages suggesting risk
stem: A client shows farewell messages drafted during a difficult night but never sent. They say they feel embarrassed. Which question best assesses whether the writing reflected preparation for self-harm?
options: Were you preparing to end your life when you wrote these?
Who did you plan to send each of these messages to?
Have you written emotional letters during difficult times before?
Which person on your support list would you like to contact?
why: Directly asking about the purpose of the drafts clarifies possible preparatory behaviour; the answer then informs assessment of current thoughts, intent and safety. Unsent drafts still warrant assessment.
Recipients provide context but do not establish the intent behind writing or present danger.
Past writing habits may inform the history but cannot establish the meaning of this episode.
Support contact can be useful, but current intent should be explored directly rather than inferred from willingness to connect.
takeaway: Assess the meaning of preparatory or farewell communication.
learningObjective: Assess the meaning of preparatory or farewell communication.

title: A support person's role
stem: A client wants a sibling to check in each evening as part of a suicide safety plan. The sibling agrees to call the crisis team if the client reports an urge to act on suicidal thoughts. Which question best verifies preparation for this role?
options: Which evenings are usually easiest for you to telephone?
Would you prefer keeping the contact numbers on paper or your phone?
Have you helped another family member through distress before?
What would you say and do if that urge is reported during a call?
why: Scheduling supports feasibility but does not demonstrate the planned response to the warning sign.
Contact format matters, but does not establish that the sibling understands the trigger and action.
Experience may inform support needs, but does not verify this specific agreed role.
A brief scenario lets the sibling demonstrate recognition, response and help-seeking using the actual plan.
takeaway: Define concrete support roles without transferring all responsibility to family.
learningObjective: Define concrete support roles without transferring all responsibility to family.

title: Crisis resources in Canada
stem: Which statements about a Canadian client's crisis-contact plan are appropriate? Select all that apply.
options: Call or text 9-8-8 for suicide crisis support
Use emergency services when immediate safety is at risk
Use 9-8-8 instead of emergency services during an immediate life-threatening event
Keep contact methods in a format the client can access
why: Canada's 9-8-8 service offers around-the-clock crisis support.
Immediate danger requires an emergency response.
Suicide crisis support does not replace emergency medical response when life is immediately threatened.
Usability matters when concentration and coping are impaired.
takeaway: Distinguish crisis support from emergency response and make contacts accessible.
learningObjective: Distinguish crisis support from emergency response and make contacts accessible.

title: Suicide risk after an acute loss
stem: An intoxicated client who lost housing yesterday says, "Nothing matters; I may as well die." They are awake, breathing normally and physically stable, but cannot sustain a full interview. Which plan is appropriate now?
options: Complete the risk interview after sobriety and decide observation then
Provide current protection and medical assessment, then reassess as alertness improves
Begin housing applications and review the statement after accommodation is found
Offer supportive counselling and arrange a follow-up appointment tomorrow
why: A fuller later interview is needed, but current protection should not wait for sobriety.
Immediate safety and physical needs can be addressed while arranging a more reliable repeated assessment as intoxication resolves.
Housing is a major practical need but does not first address the current self-harm statement and impaired assessment.
Counselling and follow-up alone do not establish a safe plan during the current intoxication and expressed risk.
takeaway: Provide immediate safety care when intoxication limits a complete suicide assessment.
learningObjective: Provide immediate safety care when intoxication limits a complete suicide assessment.

title: Risk documentation
stem: During suicide assessment, a client reports an urge to overdose, identifies medication at home and agrees to remain for urgent review. The nurse initiates the required observation and contacts the clinician. Which entry accurately summarizes the current findings and response?
options: Client agrees to stay; cooperative behaviour suggests the crisis has passed.
Client identifies home medication; family involvement will make discharge safe.
Reports overdose urge and access; observation started and urgent review requested.
Screening indicates elevated risk; plan to repeat the score after reassurance.
why: Agreement to remain does not establish that the crisis or risk has resolved.
Family involvement may help, but safe discharge has not been established from these findings.
This records the specific reported risk and actions actually taken without unsupported reassurance.
This omits the concrete findings and records a plan different from the response described.
takeaway: Document suicide-risk evidence and the actions taken.
learningObjective: Document suicide-risk evidence and the actions taken.

title: Emerging mania
stem: A client with bipolar disorder has slept very little for three nights, feels unusually energetic and has spent money needed for rent. Their previous episode began with the same pattern. What should the nurse do?
options: Arrange prompt review with the treating team
Begin sleep-hygiene coaching and review next week
Schedule the usual monthly mood follow-up
Start a mood diary for discussion at the next visit
why: The personal recurrence pattern and current financial consequence warrant prompt assessment and possible care-plan adjustment.
Sleep support can help but is insufficient as the sole response to already escalating symptoms and impaired decisions.
The routine interval may delay assessment of a meaningful current change.
Tracking is useful, but should complement rather than postpone review of the current escalation.
takeaway: Recognize reduced sleep and impulsivity as possible early mania.
learningObjective: Recognize reduced sleep and impulsivity as possible early mania.

title: Nutrition during mania
stem: A client experiencing mania has eaten little today because they leave meals after a few bites. They swallow safely and accept brief individual support. Which plan best supports intake now?
options: Provide a full plated meal in the busy dining room
Wait for the next scheduled group meal in an hour
Offer a menu and ask the client to plan the evening meal
Offer a sandwich and drink in a quiet brief supported sitting
why: The longer, more stimulating meal setting may reproduce the difficulty already limiting intake.
Waiting prolongs the identified intake deficit despite an available manageable approach.
Planning requires sustained attention and does not provide food now.
A short supported opportunity with manageable food and fluid fits the observed attention and intake needs.
takeaway: Adapt nutrition support to the activity and attention patterns of mania.
learningObjective: Adapt nutrition support to the activity and attention patterns of mania.

title: Supporting sleep in mania
stem: Which nursing actions fit a coordinated plan for a client with acute mania? Select all that apply.
options: Reduce unnecessary evening stimulation
Monitor sleep and rest patterns
Encourage late-night competitive activities to tire the client
Provide predictable brief interactions
why: Lower stimulation supports an environment more compatible with rest.
Sleep trends inform severity and treatment response.
Competition and stimulation may intensify activation.
Predictable concise contact reduces overload and conflict.
takeaway: Support rest through environmental adaptation and monitoring during mania.
learningObjective: Support rest through environmental adaptation and monitoring during mania.

title: Limit setting during mania
stem: A client with mania is about to enter another client's bedroom again. No threat is occurring. Which response provides the clearest immediate boundary?
options: Let us talk about how the other client felt when you entered earlier.
This is their private room; come with me to the lounge.
We can arrange a suitable social visit later in the day.
We will review the unit privacy rules in the next group meeting.
why: Explaining impact may help later, but requires more processing before stopping the immediate boundary crossing.
A short concrete limit and appropriate destination address the action now without shaming the client.
Planning a later visit does not clearly address the room entry occurring now.
A later group discussion does not provide the needed immediate direction.
takeaway: Use brief consistent boundaries with a concrete alternative during mania.
learningObjective: Use brief consistent boundaries with a concrete alternative during mania.

title: Impulsive financial decisions
stem: A hospitalized client with marked manic distractibility wants to make a large nonurgent purchase and cannot stay with discussion of its financial consequences. What is the most appropriate immediate nursing proposal?
options: Complete a detailed monthly budgeting worksheet together
Call a chosen supporter to discuss which product is best
Suggest a pause while the team reviews decision-support needs
Provide written purchase details for the client to compare now
why: A worksheet may help later but requires sustained processing the client currently cannot demonstrate.
Support can be valuable, but discussing product choice does not address difficulty considering consequences.
A reversible pause allows assessment and support without assuming the diagnosis itself removes financial capacity.
More detail does not resolve the observed current decision-making difficulty.
takeaway: Address impulsive high-impact decisions through delay and appropriate assessment.
learningObjective: Address impulsive high-impact decisions through delay and appropriate assessment.

title: Communication with pressured speech
stem: A client with mania speaks rapidly and changes topics when the nurse asks, "Tell me about your sleep over the past week." What approach best helps obtain this information?
options: Ask one brief sleep question and gently redirect to it
Invite an uninterrupted account of the whole previous day
Provide a full written history form to complete
Repeat the original open-ended question at the same length
why: A concrete limited question with calm redirection matches the current attention difficulty.
A broad narrative may increase topic shifts before obtaining the needed detail.
A full form adds processing demands and may not fit current distractibility.
Repeating the same broad demand does not adapt to the observed difficulty.
takeaway: Keep communication concrete and focused during manic distractibility.
learningObjective: Keep communication concrete and focused during manic distractibility.

title: Family plan for bipolar recurrence
stem: With the client's agreement, a family bipolar-care plan directs contacting the team after two nights of markedly reduced sleep plus renewed impulsive spending. The family observes both changes today. Which response applies the plan?
options: Continue the sleep diary until the next scheduled appointment
Ask the client to spend the weekend resting before calling
Review the family budget together before deciding on contact
Contact the agreed team now and describe the observed changes
why: Records are useful but the specified contact threshold has already been reached.
Rest support may help, but does not replace the agreed response to this combination.
Financial support can be part of care but should not delay the planned clinical contact.
The actual observations meet the individualized threshold, making the agreed team contact appropriate.
takeaway: Build bipolar relapse plans around the client's own early warning pattern.
learningObjective: Build bipolar relapse plans around the client's own early warning pattern.

title: Evaluating mania improvement
stem: Which findings suggest improvement in a client treated for mania? Select all that apply.
options: Longer sustained sleep periods
Better ability to remain with a simple task
Increased impulsive spending plans
Improved food and fluid intake
why: Restoring sleep can indicate reduced activation.
Improved attention supports meaningful functional recovery.
Growing impulsivity suggests continuing impaired judgment.
Improved intake addresses a common physical consequence of mania.
takeaway: Evaluate manic recovery through sleep, attention, judgment and basic needs.
learningObjective: Evaluate manic recovery through sleep, attention, judgment and basic needs.

title: Mood tracking for bipolar disorder
stem: A stable client with bipolar disorder wants to recognize a pattern in which shorter sleep precedes rising energy and spending. Which daily record best helps identify that sequence?
options: Sleep hours, mood, energy and spending changes with dates
Meal times, daily weight and appetite changes with dates
Medication times, doses and refill dates each month
Weekly appointment dates and topics discussed at each visit
why: Dated tracking of the relevant variables can show their order and relationship over time.
Nutrition measures matter in care but do not directly capture the recurrence pattern described.
Medication records are useful but do not document the sleep-to-activation sequence.
Visit records show service contact rather than the daily progression of the warning pattern.
takeaway: Track mood alongside sleep, activity and context in bipolar care.
learningObjective: Track mood alongside sleep, activity and context in bipolar care.

title: Feeling well and treatment continuation
stem: A client with bipolar disorder feels well and wants to stop follow-up, saying, "I thought appointments were for when I am ill." Which response best supports an informed decision?
options: You could return when the early warning signs begin again.
Follow-up also supports staying well; what concerns do you have about continuing?
We can focus future visits on whether you need another prescription.
We can schedule visits farther apart while you feel well.
why: Symptom-triggered contact is useful but does not explain preventive review during stability.
Explaining the maintenance purpose while exploring concerns supports a shared review rather than automatic cessation.
Prescription access is one function, but narrowing visits to refills misses broader maintenance needs.
Spacing may be considered collaboratively, but does not first clarify the client's misunderstanding about the purpose of follow-up during wellness.
takeaway: Explain the purpose of maintenance care during bipolar stability.
learningObjective: Explain the purpose of maintenance care during bipolar stability.

title: Depressive and activated symptoms together
stem: A physically stable client reports hopelessness while pacing, sleeping little and describing racing thoughts. Which assessment is the immediate priority?
options: How many hours of sleep occurred on each recent night?
What purchases have been made during the past week?
Are there current thoughts of suicide, intent or a plan?
Were the prescribed medicines taken on schedule this week?
why: Sleep history helps characterize the mood pattern but does not establish current self-harm risk.
Impulsivity matters to the broader assessment but is secondary to the combined hopelessness and activation cue.
Direct safety inquiry is needed because activation does not protect against risk associated with hopelessness.
Medication history informs treatment review but should not postpone direct assessment of current danger.
takeaway: Escalate hopelessness accompanied by activation or agitation.
learningObjective: Escalate hopelessness accompanied by activation or agitation.

title: Distinguishing reduced need from insomnia
stem: A client sleeps two hours nightly yet feels fully rested, unusually powerful and ready to start several major projects. Which interpretation best fits this sleep report?
options: Reduced need for sleep accompanying mood activation
Insomnia producing daytime exhaustion and impaired energy
A delayed sleep phase with adequate sleep later in the day
Worry-related sleep loss followed by fatigue and desire for more rest
why: Rested high energy despite very little sleep, together with grandiosity and activation, differs from inability to sleep while tired.
The client reports feeling rested and highly energetic rather than exhausted.
The scenario does not describe obtaining normal sleep at a later time.
Worry-related sleep loss commonly includes wanting sleep and fatigue, which differ from the stated pattern.
takeaway: Assess reduced sleep need together with energy and judgment changes.
learningObjective: Assess reduced sleep need together with energy and judgment changes.

title: Protecting dignity during disinhibition
stem: A client with mania makes another sexual comment to a peer who looks uncomfortable. No physical threat is occurring. Which response best addresses the current boundary?
options: Explain at length how comments can affect relationships
Ask the peer to describe how the comment made them feel
Offer a different activity for the whole group
State that sexual comments must stop and redirect privately
why: A lengthy explanation may exceed current attention and delays a clear immediate limit.
The peer should not have to manage the boundary through a confrontation.
Changing activities may redirect attention but leaves the expected behaviour unclear.
A brief respectful limit addresses the behaviour while private redirection preserves dignity and protects the peer.
takeaway: Address disinhibition with dignity, limits and coordinated reassessment.
learningObjective: Address disinhibition with dignity, limits and coordinated reassessment.

title: Selecting manageable activities
stem: A client recovering from mania can focus for about five minutes with simple cues but loses track of multistep games. Which elements fit the next activity plan? Select all that apply.
options: A brief card-sorting task with a staff cue as needed
A quiet drawing activity with two available materials
A competitive strategy game requiring several planned moves
A short rest opportunity between activities
why: A simple time-limited task matches the observed capacity.
Low stimulation and limited choice reduce processing demands while preserving activity.
The multistep competitive task exceeds the current ability described.
Planned rests can prevent the schedule from exceeding present endurance and attention.
takeaway: Match activity complexity and stimulation to current manic recovery.
learningObjective: Match activity complexity and stimulation to current manic recovery.

title: Food-related suspiciousness
stem: A client with psychosis has skipped lunch because of fears that food was tampered with. They say they will accept intact packaged portions, which are available now. What is the most feasible immediate meal plan?
options: Ask staff to taste the served meal in front of the client
Offer sealed portions for the client to open
Ask a relative to bring a meal later this evening
Explain the kitchen's food-safety inspection process
why: Tasting can become reassurance linked to the belief and may not make the meal acceptable.
The available acceptable food addresses current intake without agreeing that the other food is poisoned.
A familiar meal may help later, but delays nourishment when an acceptable option is ready.
Factual information can be offered, but may not address the immediate barrier as effectively as the accepted food option.
takeaway: Support basic needs without validating a delusion.
learningObjective: Support basic needs without validating a delusion.

title: Thought blocking in conversation
stem: A client answering fluently suddenly stops mid-sentence and says, "The thought is gone." What should the nurse do first?
options: Finish the sentence using the likely meaning
Repeat the question immediately in the same words
Allow a pause, then ask whether the client wants to continue
Give a written list of possible answers to select
why: Finishing may substitute the nurse's assumption for the client's intended meaning.
Immediate repetition can add pressure before the client has time to recover the thought.
Time and a gentle readiness check respond to the sudden interruption without forcing or assuming content.
Choices may support a later difficulty but prematurely narrow the possible response.
takeaway: Allow time and clarify sudden interruptions in thought.
learningObjective: Allow time and clarify sudden interruptions in thought.

title: Distinguishing a tangential response
stem: Asked what time they went to sleep, a client speaks at a normal pace: "Sleep reminds me of bedrooms. My old room had blue walls. Blue paint is expensive now." Similar replies move away from each question and never give the requested information. Which description best fits this pattern?
options: Tangential responses that do not return to the question
Circumstantial responses that eventually reach the answer
Pressured speech with rapid flight from one idea to another
Thought blocking with abrupt interruption of speech
why: The repeated drift away from the requested point without answering supports a tangential pattern.
Circumstantial speech includes extra detail but eventually returns to the point, unlike the described replies.
The normal pace and absence of pressured delivery do not fit rapid flight of ideas as well.
Speech continues; there is no abrupt loss or cessation of the train of thought.
takeaway: Describe the observed thought pattern using how the response relates to the question.
learningObjective: Describe the observed thought pattern using how the response relates to the question.

title: New reduced alertness during routine care
stem: A client with schizophrenia usually needs prompts to begin hygiene but then performs it safely. Today the nurse also notices new drowsiness, slower walking and difficulty staying awake after a medicine change. What should happen next?
options: Increase the frequency of the usual hygiene prompts
Complete hygiene earlier before the client lies down
Continue the familiar routine and compare it tomorrow
Assess the new alertness change and seek a medication review
why: More prompts do not evaluate the new sedation and slowed movement.
Timing changes may support a stable routine but do not explain a new post-change presentation.
Waiting may miss a clinically significant treatment effect or another cause.
The new deviation from baseline warrants assessment of possible medication effects and other causes before treating it as usual low initiation.
takeaway: Assess a new change in alertness and function rather than treating it as baseline low initiation.
subtopic: New functional change during mental-health treatment
learningObjective: Assess a new change in alertness and function rather than treating it as baseline low initiation.

title: Assessing hallucination impact
stem: A client says a voice is telling them to hurt a neighbour. Which questions most directly assess the immediate risk of acting on the command? Select all that apply.
options: What exactly is the voice telling you to do?
Do you feel that you might act on what it says?
When did you first hear a voice in your life?
How able do you feel to resist the instruction now?
Which settings usually make the voices more noticeable?
why: The specific command establishes the potential action and target for focused safety assessment.
Current likelihood or intent to comply directly informs immediate risk.
Onset informs the history but is less direct for current command-related danger.
Perceived control or ability to resist helps determine present protection needs.
Triggers can guide longer-term coping but do not directly establish whether the client may act now.
takeaway: Assess hallucination content, commands and behavioural effects.
learningObjective: Assess hallucination content, commands and behavioural effects.

title: Coping with noncommand voices
stem: A client with distressing noncommand voices chooses quiet music during a simple craft task. Which follow-up finding best supports continuing this coping strategy?
options: The client keeps the music on throughout the session
Distress falls and the client resumes the chosen task
The client names several other available coping strategies
The client describes the music as familiar from childhood
why: Use alone does not show whether the strategy improves distress or functioning.
Improved comfort with resumed activity demonstrates a useful effect; continue reassessing symptoms and safety.
Knowledge of alternatives may help planning but does not evaluate the selected music strategy.
Familiarity may matter to preference but does not by itself establish clinical benefit.
takeaway: Evaluate individualized coping strategies for distressing hallucinations.
learningObjective: Evaluate individualized coping strategies for distressing hallucinations.

title: Physical deterioration after fear-related fluid refusal
stem: A client with psychosis has refused most drinks because they fear an open jug was tampered with and has also vomited repeatedly. The nurse offers acceptable sealed drinks and assesses physical status. Which additional finding requires emergency medical escalation?
options: Dry lips with alert conversation and usual urine output
Mild thirst while drinking an offered sealed beverage
Near-fainting on standing with almost no urine for twelve hours
Nausea after drinking while remaining steady when walking
why: Dry lips need assessment and intake support, but preserved alertness and output lack the severe perfusion cues.
Thirst and accepting fluids warrant continued monitoring but do not indicate the same acute compromise.
Severe dizziness and prolonged markedly reduced urine after poor intake and vomiting suggest serious dehydration or another circulatory problem requiring emergency assessment.
Nausea needs ongoing care, but the described stable mobility is less urgent than near-syncope with minimal output.
takeaway: Recognize physical compromise when psychotic fears interfere with adequate intake.
learningObjective: Recognize physical compromise when psychotic fears interfere with adequate intake.

title: Distractibility during self-care teaching
stem: A client recovering from psychosis can brush their teeth when each step is prompted, but loses track when the whole sequence is explained. Which teaching approach best builds on the observed ability?
options: Guide practice through one step at a time
Demonstrate the complete routine before the client begins
Provide a written sequence to study after the session
Ask the caregiver to complete the routine for the client
why: Brief cues with immediate practice match the demonstrated attention limit and preserve participation.
A full demonstration still requires retaining the complete sequence before acting.
Written information may support later recall but does not provide the currently effective stepwise practice.
Caregiver completion meets the task need but does not build the client's demonstrated ability to perform it.
takeaway: Break self-care learning into manageable steps during psychosis recovery.
learningObjective: Break self-care learning into manageable steps during psychosis recovery.

title: Delusional fear of assessment
stem: A client believes a blood-pressure cuff reads thoughts and refuses a nonurgent measurement. Which response best begins exploring the fear while respecting the refusal?
options: This cuff measures pressure; many clients find that explanation reassuring.
We could talk about your breakfast while I prepare the equipment.
The measurement will help your treatment, so please consider having it done.
You seem worried; what concerns you about using the cuff?
why: Factual information is useful, but reassurance alone may not reveal the specific concern.
Changing the subject does not address the refusal or obtain agreement to proceed.
Explaining benefit may help informed choice but begins persuasion before exploring the fear.
Acknowledging emotion and inviting the client's account allows clarification without validating the thought-reading belief.
takeaway: Address fear and negotiate nonurgent care without endorsing delusions.
learningObjective: Address fear and negotiate nonurgent care without endorsing delusions.

title: Early psychosis change
stem: A young adult previously attended college reliably and socialized regularly. Which newly reported changes warrant timely assessment for a possible emerging mental-health problem? Select all that apply.
options: Over six weeks, increasing fear of being watched has led to missed classes
New voices commenting on actions are distressing and interrupt study
A late examination night is followed by one tired day and usual sleep
A preference for studying alone continues with usual grades and friendships
Brief worry before an oral presentation settles after the presentation
why: Persistent suspiciousness with functional decline is a meaningful change requiring assessment.
Distressing new perceptual experiences that interfere with function warrant assessment.
A brief understandable response followed by recovery does not show the sustained change described in the keyed findings.
A stable preference with maintained function is not by itself evidence of emerging psychosis.
Transient situational anxiety that settles lacks the persistent functional and perceptual change of concern.
takeaway: Assess emerging perceptual or thought changes that impair functioning.
learningObjective: Assess emerging perceptual or thought changes that impair functioning.

title: A belief and cultural context
stem: A client describes sensing a deceased relative's presence during a culturally meaningful mourning practice. The nurse has established its accepted spiritual meaning but does not know how it affects the client. Which question best clarifies clinical significance?
options: How long has this mourning practice been part of your family?
Is the experience distressing or interfering with your daily life?
Which relatives usually take part in the mourning practice?
Would you like information about the clinic's spiritual-care service?
why: History adds context, but accepted meaning has already been established.
Distress and impairment help distinguish a meaningful experience from one requiring further clinical assessment; associated symptoms can then be explored.
Participants may identify supports, but do not establish the effect on this client.
Spiritual care may be welcome, but offering it does not clarify the current clinical impact.
takeaway: Assess spiritual experiences within cultural and functional context.
learningObjective: Assess spiritual experiences within cultural and functional context.

title: Risk and diagnosis
stem: A client with schizophrenia usually hears noncommand voices, avoids crowded groups and sometimes sleeps poorly. Which new finding most clearly requires revising the immediate violence-safety plan?
options: The client declines today's large discussion group
The client reports distress from the usual voices
The client threatens a named person and describes an available weapon
The client slept five hours instead of the usual seven
why: A familiar group preference does not by itself establish new violent intent.
Distress deserves support and assessment, but the reported familiar experience is less specific than a targeted threat with means.
A specific threat and access require immediate focused risk assessment and protective response.
Reduced sleep is relevant context but does not alone carry the same immediate significance as the stated threat.
takeaway: Assess behaviour and context rather than stereotyping psychiatric diagnosis.
learningObjective: Assess behaviour and context rather than stereotyping psychiatric diagnosis.

title: Suspiciousness during handoff
stem: A client becomes suspicious after hearing two nurses whisper about their care at handoff and asks, "What are you saying about me?" What response best addresses the immediate concern?
options: Explain the relevant care discussion privately and invite questions
Move the handoff farther away and finish it first
Reassure the client that the nurses are trying to help
Promise to discuss the handoff at the next scheduled meeting
why: Transparent relevant information in an appropriate setting directly addresses the worry while protecting confidentiality.
Relocation improves privacy but leaves the client's expressed concern unexplained.
General reassurance does not clarify what was said and may not reduce the specific mistrust.
Delayed discussion leaves a presently answerable concern unresolved.
takeaway: Reduce avoidable ambiguity while preserving confidentiality.
learningObjective: Reduce avoidable ambiguity while preserving confidentiality.

title: A client stands motionless
stem: A client with a severe mood disorder has newly remained almost motionless for most of the day, responds minimally and has taken very little fluid. Their mouth is dry and pulse is 112/min. What should the nurse prioritize?
options: Offer small amounts of fluid and review intake at the next round
Increase routine observation of the behaviour over the evening
Arrange a supportive interview about low motivation
Obtain prompt clinical assessment and escalate the physical findings
why: Intake support may be needed, but minimal responsiveness and physical changes require assessment before relying on oral encouragement.
Observation alone delays evaluation of a marked change and possible dehydration or other illness.
A motivation-focused approach may misattribute a syndrome requiring medical assessment.
New severe reduction in movement and response with poor intake raises concern for catatonia or another acute cause with physical compromise.
takeaway: Escalate marked motor withdrawal with reduced responsiveness or intake.
learningObjective: Escalate marked motor withdrawal with reduced responsiveness or intake.

title: Recovery goals in psychosis
stem: A client with persistent but manageable voices wants to volunteer at a library and choose their own weekly routine. Which outcomes directly demonstrate progress in participation and self-management? Select all that apply.
options: Completes a chosen half-hour library task with agreed support
Uses an agreed coping pause and returns to the library task
Reports a lower voice-intensity score during a clinic interview
Selects feasible volunteer hours and communicates the choice
Receives information about three community programmes
why: Actual participation in the chosen activity demonstrates functional progress.
Applying coping in the activity supports sustained participation despite symptoms.
Symptom reduction is useful, but this observation does not by itself demonstrate the specified activity or decision-making goal.
Choosing and communicating a workable routine demonstrates agency in the stated goal.
Information is a service input, not evidence that the client has yet participated or used a self-management skill.
takeaway: Define recovery through the client's goals, agency and functioning.
learningObjective: Define recovery through the client's goals, agency and functioning.

title: Family education about hallucinations
stem: A relative hearing voices appears frightened and asks a caregiver for help. Which caregiver response best acknowledges distress and opens assessment of immediate help needs?
options: The room is quiet; let us check together where the sound could come from.
You look frightened; are the voices telling you to do something unsafe?
You have coped with this before; remind yourself that it usually settles.
Let us watch a familiar programme and see whether you feel better.
why: Trying to locate the sound may shift the discussion toward proving or disproving the experience rather than current distress and risk.
Acknowledging emotion and asking about harmful commands helps identify whether urgent support is needed without claiming to hear the voices.
Encouragement may help, but past coping does not establish the safety of the current experience.
Distraction may be useful once help needs are understood, but does not first clarify current danger.
takeaway: Teach family to acknowledge distress without confirming hallucinations.
learningObjective: Teach family to acknowledge distress without confirming hallucinations.

title: Daily function after psychosis
stem: A client wants to resume preparing a hot lunch. During practice, they complete each step but leave a heating pan when distracted by conversation. What is the best next practice plan?
options: Add written reminders and repeat the whole meal independently
Have the caregiver prepare the hot portion while the client watches
Practise one-pan cooking with direct support and fewer distractions
Substitute a cold lunch prepared by the caregiver each day
why: Reminders may help, but current performance does not yet establish safe independent use of heat.
Observation can help learning, but provides less opportunity to practise the steps the client can perform.
Supported graded practice targets the observed distraction hazard while retaining the client's chosen skill goal.
A cold meal can be safe, but caregiver completion does not build the requested cooking ability.
takeaway: Assess real-world task performance during psychosis recovery.
learningObjective: Assess real-world task performance during psychosis recovery.

title: Unwanted discussion of diagnosis
stem: A capable client has asked staff not to share clinical information with a visiting friend. The friend asks which diagnosis and medicines explain the admission. Which reply respects the boundary?
options: I can discuss general visiting arrangements; clinical questions require the client's permission.
I can explain the diagnosis while leaving the medication names private.
I can describe the medication group rather than the individual prescriptions.
I can summarize the treatment goal because you are here to offer support.
why: General service information can be shared while preserving the client's explicit boundary on personal clinical details.
The diagnosis remains client-specific clinical information covered by the refusal.
A medication class still reveals personal treatment information.
Supportive visiting does not establish permission to disclose the client's treatment goals.
takeaway: Clarify consent before sharing mental-health information with visitors.
learningObjective: Clarify consent before sharing mental-health information with visitors.

title: Housing stability and recovery
stem: A client recovering from psychosis moves between shelters, has no reliable phone and repeatedly loses contact with the same treatment team. They use a day centre each Tuesday and agree to its involvement. Which plan best maintains the treatment connection?
options: Book the usual clinic appointment and mail reminders to the last shelter
Ask the client to telephone when they know their next address
Arrange a new clinic referral whenever accommodation changes
Agree on a regular day-centre contact with the current outreach team
why: An old mailing address does not provide a dependable contact route across moves.
Waiting for a new address may prolong disconnection for someone without reliable telephone access.
Repeated referrals can fragment the existing therapeutic connection and do not solve the contact problem.
An agreed stable location and continuing team provide a feasible connection despite changes in sleeping accommodation.
takeaway: Address housing-related barriers when planning mental-health follow-up.
learningObjective: Address housing-related barriers when planning mental-health follow-up.

title: Memory supports for appointment attendance
stem: A client recovering from psychosis understands the purpose and dates of appointments but forgets them during the week. They manage a smartphone independently, check the noticeboard beside their keys daily and want to attend independently. Which additions most directly compensate for the reported memory difficulty? Select all that apply.
options: Enter agreed reminders in the phone calendar
Repeat a longer explanation of the service at each visit
Place a clear appointment cue beside the keys
Ask a relative to book the appointments for the client
Provide a detailed leaflet about the benefits of follow-up
why: Time-linked prompts use a tool the client already manages to cue the intended action.
The purpose is already understood; additional explanation does not directly provide a cue when the appointment is approaching.
A visible reminder at an established daily stopping point links the information to an existing routine.
Changing who books the visit does not address remembering the agreed date during the week.
More information about benefits does not directly compensate for the described prospective-memory difficulty.
takeaway: Match practical environmental prompts to the specific cognitive difficulty and the client's established routines.
learningObjective: Match practical environmental prompts to the specific cognitive difficulty and the client's established routines.

title: Alcohol history before admission
stem: Before a planned surgical admission, a client reports daily heavy drinking and a previous withdrawal seizure. They currently have no withdrawal symptoms. What should the nurse prioritize?
options: Begin routine symptom scoring after admission and report rising scores
Communicate the seizure history now for a monitored prevention plan
Arrange a community alcohol-service referral for after discharge
Complete the usual fasting and postoperative breathing teaching
why: Monitoring is necessary, but prior complicated withdrawal warrants a prospective plan before symptoms appear.
The history identifies increased withdrawal risk that the team should address in the admission plan.
Longer-term support matters but does not prepare for withdrawal during the impending admission.
Usual surgical teaching remains useful but does not address the high-risk history.
takeaway: Identify severe withdrawal history before alcohol use is interrupted.
learningObjective: Identify severe withdrawal history before alcohol use is interrupted.

title: Substance-use interviewing
stem: A client is embarrassed about discussing alcohol before admission. The nurse needs information to estimate withdrawal risk. Which respectful question provides the most directly relevant starting information?
options: How has drinking affected your work or relationships recently?
What changes in your drinking would you like to make?
What do you drink, how much, and when was your last drink?
How do people close to you feel about your drinking?
why: Consequences inform the broader assessment but do not establish current exposure and time since cessation.
Readiness guides longer-term goals but does not quantify immediate withdrawal risk.
Recent pattern and last use guide risk assessment, alongside prior withdrawal history and clinical findings.
Family perspectives may help, but are less direct than the recent amount and timing.
takeaway: Ask neutral specific questions about substance use.
learningObjective: Ask neutral specific questions about substance use.

title: Intoxication and an injury history
stem: A drowsy client who smells of alcohol arrives after an unwitnessed fall. Which action takes priority?
options: Assess airway, neurologic status and possible injury promptly
Obtain a detailed account of usual drinking patterns first
Arrange transport home once a relative answers the phone
Recheck alertness after an uninterrupted period of sleep
why: Intoxication can coexist with serious injury and must not explain away reduced responsiveness.
Substance history is useful but does not precede immediate physical assessment.
A ride home does not establish medical stability after a fall.
Waiting for sleep can delay recognition of injury or airway compromise.
takeaway: Assess injury and physiologic stability before attributing drowsiness to alcohol.
learningObjective: Assess injury and physiologic stability before attributing drowsiness to alcohol.

title: Withdrawal and a scoring tool
stem: During monitored alcohol withdrawal, a client becomes more tremulous and diaphoretic but remains oriented. The documented protocol directs immediate clinician notification when symptoms worsen and pulse exceeds 110/min; pulse is now 116/min. No rescue dose is authorized. What should the nurse do?
options: Repeat the full assessment at the next routine hourly interval
Offer fluids and recheck the pulse after a rest period
Increase observations to every 15 minutes
Notify the clinician now with the assessment findings
why: The stated escalation threshold has been met, so waiting for the routine interval delays the required response.
Supportive care may continue, but should not postpone notification of worsening signs above the defined threshold.
Closer monitoring may be needed, but does not replace the indicated clinician notification once the stated threshold has been met.
Prompt communication follows the supplied protocol and allows an authorized treatment decision.
takeaway: Respond to worsening withdrawal using both clinical assessment and authorized protocols.
learningObjective: Respond to worsening withdrawal using both clinical assessment and authorized protocols.

title: Severe withdrawal warning findings
stem: During alcohol-withdrawal monitoring, which new findings require urgent escalation rather than continued routine reassessment? Select all that apply.
options: New disorientation with marked agitation
A generalized seizure
Mild nausea while retaining fluids and remaining oriented
A mild stable hand tremor with unchanged vital signs
Anxiety that eases with reassurance and a quieter setting
why: Acute confusion and marked agitation can indicate severe withdrawal or another acute cause requiring urgent assessment.
A seizure requires immediate safety care and urgent clinical response.
Nausea still requires monitoring and treatment as indicated, but the described stable state lacks the urgent neurological deterioration.
Stable mild tremor needs protocol monitoring but does not carry the same emergency significance as seizure or new confusion.
Settling anxiety without deterioration is less urgent than the neurological changes identified.
takeaway: Escalate neurologic changes and marked instability during alcohol withdrawal.
learningObjective: Escalate neurologic changes and marked instability during alcohol withdrawal.

title: Withdrawal recovery versus addiction treatment
stem: A client has completed medically supervised alcohol withdrawal and asks what follow-up will help with ongoing recovery. Which plan best addresses that purpose?
options: Arrange continuing alcohol-use treatment matched to goals and supports
Arrange a liver-function blood test at the usual clinic
Provide instructions to return if tremor develops again
Book a routine annual physical examination
why: Withdrawal management addresses an acute phase; continuing treatment can address use patterns, cravings, goals and sustained support.
Physical monitoring is useful but does not constitute a continuing alcohol-use treatment plan.
Symptom instructions support safety but wait for a problem rather than establish ongoing recovery care.
General preventive care matters but does not directly address the current recovery needs.
takeaway: Link withdrawal stabilization with ongoing treatment and recovery planning.
learningObjective: Link withdrawal stabilization with ongoing treatment and recovery planning.

title: A return to drinking
stem: A client resumed drinking after several months of abstinence and avoided follow-up because of shame. Which opening best supports a current assessment?
options: You made progress before; let us restart exactly the same treatment.
What has drinking been like recently, and what was happening when it resumed?
Many people have setbacks; try not to dwell on this episode.
Which date would you choose for your next period of abstinence?
why: Prior treatment may still help, but should be reviewed in light of the current pattern and circumstances.
A neutral invitation supports disclosure of current exposure, safety needs and relevant triggers.
Reassurance may reduce shame but can bypass understanding what has changed.
Goal-setting is useful after exploring current needs and the client's preferences.
takeaway: Use recurrence to reassess safety, triggers and support needs.
learningObjective: Use recurrence to reassess safety, triggers and support needs.

title: Alcohol and sedating medication
stem: A client takes a prescribed benzodiazepine at bedtime and also drinks alcohol to fall asleep. Which teaching addresses the main safety concern?
options: Leave a two-hour interval between the drink and the medicine
Keep the usual medicine dose when choosing a lower-alcohol drink
Combined sedation can be dangerous; review the alcohol and medicine plan
Skip each medicine dose on evenings when alcohol is used
why: A short interval does not reliably prevent overlapping sedative effects.
Lower alcohol concentration does not establish safe combined exposure; total intake and the medicine both matter.
Additive central nervous system depression can impair safety and breathing; a professional review should guide changes rather than abrupt self-adjustment.
Self-directed skipping may cause other harms, including withdrawal with some patterns of benzodiazepine use; the regimen needs review.
takeaway: Assess and address combined depressant exposure.
learningObjective: Assess and address combined depressant exposure.

title: Exploring readiness for change
stem: A client says, "Reducing alcohol might help my family, but I do not know how I would manage stress." Which reply best explores this ambivalence?
options: You want family life to improve and worry about losing a coping method.
Alcohol can worsen stress over time; shall I explain how that happens?
You could try walking when stressed instead of having a drink.
Let us choose a smaller number of drinks for tomorrow evening.
why: Reflecting both values invites the client to explore the tension and possible alternatives in their own terms.
Education can be helpful but moves away from first understanding the two concerns expressed.
A suggested alternative may help later but assumes a suitable strategy before exploring preferences.
Action planning may be premature while the client is expressing uncertainty about coping.
takeaway: Explore the benefits and barriers the client identifies in changing substance use.
learningObjective: Explore the benefits and barriers the client identifies in changing substance use.

title: Recovery and meaningful routines
stem: A client in early recovery reports that the old evening drinking group triggers urges. They enjoy walking, and a trusted friend is available for a short evening walk near home. Which plan best fits the current need?
options: Meet the old group briefly and order a nonalcoholic drink
Watch television alone through the usual drinking hours
Save planned social activity for the next weekend
Arrange the evening walk with the trusted friend
why: This keeps the client in the identified high-risk setting during early recovery.
Distraction may help but offers less of the valued activity and available support described.
Weekend plans leave the identified recurring evening period unaddressed.
The accessible valued activity provides support during the specific time and away from the identified cue.
takeaway: Plan meaningful alternatives for times previously organized around substance use.
learningObjective: Plan meaningful alternatives for times previously organized around substance use.

title: Respectful substance-use documentation
stem: A client reports opioid use yesterday at 20:00, declines a referral after discussion and requests review of abdominal pain rated 7/10. Which notes accurately document this encounter? Select all that apply.
options: Reports last opioid use yesterday at approximately 20:00
Declined the offered referral after options were discussed
Requests analgesia because opioid use has increased pain sensitivity
Requests review of abdominal pain rated 7/10
Declined referral because further treatment is not a priority
why: This records the client's reported exposure and timing.
This describes the observed decision and discussion without assigning a motive.
The causal explanation has not been established by the stated encounter.
This records the symptom report, location and rating rather than judging its legitimacy.
The reason for declining was not supplied and should not be inferred.
takeaway: Document substance-use information and behaviour without judgmental labels.
learningObjective: Document substance-use information and behaviour without judgmental labels.

title: Pain with opioid-use disorder
stem: A postoperative client receiving ongoing treatment for opioid-use disorder reports pain of 8/10 despite the authorized analgesia and repositioning. They are alert, with respiratory rate 16/min and oxygen saturation 97%. What should the nurse do next?
options: Continue comfort measures until the next scheduled analgesic dose
Coordinate prompt review of the pain and opioid-use treatment plans
Request replacement of the maintenance treatment with an analgesic regimen
Reassess the pain after the client has had a period of sleep
why: Comfort measures may continue, but severe persisting pain after the available regimen requires review.
The current response and respiratory assessment support timely coordinated pain review while preserving appropriate addiction treatment.
Replacing maintenance treatment is not an automatic solution and may disrupt care; the teams should coordinate an individualized plan.
Waiting for sleep delays response to an already assessed inadequate analgesic effect.
takeaway: Assess and treat pain without diagnostic stigma.
learningObjective: Assess and treat pain without diagnostic stigma.

title: Naloxone follow-up teaching
stem: After take-home naloxone teaching, a family member describes what they would do if a person wakes after a dose. Which plan shows appropriate follow-through?
options: Stay at home and check breathing until the person feels normal
Call a pharmacist for advice if the person remains awake
Keep emergency help activated and monitor until responders take over
Call emergency help if sleepiness returns after the initial recovery
why: Home observation does not replace emergency assessment after suspected opioid poisoning.
A pharmacist can support education but is not the emergency response required after an overdose.
The improvement may be temporary, so continued monitoring and emergency care remain necessary.
Waiting for recurrent deterioration can delay essential emergency care.
takeaway: Teach that naloxone reversal is temporary and does not replace emergency care.
learningObjective: Teach that naloxone reversal is temporary and does not replace emergency care.

title: Lower tolerance after abstinence
stem: A client leaving treatment asks whether their previous opioid amount would have the same effect after several weeks without use. Which explanation is most accurate?
options: Lower tolerance can make the previous amount more dangerous
Previous experience remains a dependable guide to the same amount
An unchanged route makes the response similar to before treatment
Drug clearance during abstinence reduces the risk from the old amount
why: Tolerance can fall during abstinence; an amount previously used can now cause greater harm, and an unpredictable supply adds further risk.
Prior experience does not account for reduced tolerance or variable contents.
Using the same route does not preserve tolerance after abstinence.
Clearing earlier doses does not preserve tolerance; renewed exposure to the previously used amount can be hazardous after abstinence.
takeaway: Discuss increased overdose risk after reduced opioid exposure.
learningObjective: Discuss increased overdose risk after reduced opioid exposure.

title: Mixed-drug overdose concern
stem: A person is unresponsive with very slow breathing after an uncertain substance exposure. Emergency help has been called and a naloxone kit is available. What should the trained responder do?
options: Ask companions to identify the substance before opening the kit
Telephone a toxicology service before choosing the next response
Reassess breathing again before deciding whether to use naloxone
Use naloxone and provide breathing support as directed by emergency guidance
why: Additional history should not delay response when opioid poisoning is reasonably suspected.
Specialist advice may be useful, but should not delay the immediate emergency instructions and available treatment.
Ongoing assessment is needed alongside prompt treatment, not as a reason to postpone it in this presentation.
Naloxone is appropriate for suspected opioid poisoning; follow kit and dispatcher instructions, including required breathing or resuscitation support.
takeaway: Respond to suspected opioid poisoning without waiting for certainty.
learningObjective: Respond to suspected opioid poisoning without waiting for certainty.

title: Planning a reachable overdose response
stem: A client who may use nonprescribed opioids usually uses alone, leaving nobody to respond if they become unresponsive. A supervised service and virtual overdose-response service are available, and the client has reliable phone service. Which arrangements directly address this response gap? Select all that apply.
options: Use the available supervised service during its operating hours
Keep a naloxone kit beside the bed while continuing to use alone
Arrange for a trained sober support person to stay and respond
Send a friend a check-in text the following morning
Connect with the virtual service and agree its emergency-response plan
why: The service provides trained people able to recognize deterioration and respond.
Having a kit is valuable, but an unresponsive person cannot reliably administer it to themselves; the responder gap remains.
An available capable person can activate emergency help and use the agreed response measures.
A next-morning message may be too late to identify and respond to an acute overdose.
A verified real-time service arrangement can monitor and activate a response; confirm access and procedure rather than assume a phone contact guarantees rescue.
takeaway: Make overdose prevention actionable by arranging someone or a service able to respond.
learningObjective: Make overdose prevention actionable by arranging someone or a service able to respond.

title: Opioid withdrawal distress
stem: After interruption of regular opioid use, an alert client develops yawning, diffuse aches, watery diarrhea and restlessness. Respirations are 18/min, oxygen saturation 98%, and they are taking little fluid because of nausea. What should the nurse prioritize?
options: Focus the interview on recent infectious contacts
Assess withdrawal severity and hydration to guide authorized support
Increase monitoring primarily for opioid-induced respiratory depression
Begin a detailed discussion of long-term recovery goals
why: Infection remains a possible alternative if indicated, but the timing and combined symptom pattern support assessing withdrawal first.
The pattern after interrupted use warrants withdrawal assessment and attention to fluid losses and intake.
Alertness and normal respirations do not suggest respiratory depression as the main current problem.
Long-term goals matter, but the current physical discomfort and losses need assessment and care now.
takeaway: Assess opioid withdrawal symptoms and physical needs promptly.
learningObjective: Assess opioid withdrawal symptoms and physical needs promptly.

title: Stimulant-related acute symptoms
stem: After recent stimulant use, a client has chest pain, a very rapid pulse, marked agitation and hot flushed skin. What is the priority?
options: Obtain a detailed timeline of the substance exposure
Offer oral fluids and move to a cooler room
Activate emergency medical assessment and support
Use a calming conversation and reassess after settling
why: Exposure history is useful, but should not delay response to potentially serious cardiovascular and temperature-related toxicity.
Cooling support may help while emergency care is arranged, but oral fluids alone do not evaluate the acute presentation.
Chest pain with marked physiological activation requires urgent medical response; reduce stimulation and maintain safety while help arrives.
Anxiety support is appropriate alongside care, but improvement in agitation would not exclude serious toxicity.
takeaway: Escalate cardiovascular and heat-related symptoms after stimulant use.
learningObjective: Escalate cardiovascular and heat-related symptoms after stimulant use.

title: Cannabis-related anxiety
stem: A client develops marked anxiety and suspiciousness an hour after using an unfamiliar cannabis concentrate. The amount and other ingredients are uncertain; their hands tremble and no vital signs have been taken. What should the nurse do first?
options: Assess physical status and immediate safety in a calm setting
Reassure the client that the experience will pass with time
Begin the client's preferred grounding exercise
Review ways to avoid another similar exposure after discharge
why: Unknown exposure and unevaluated physical signs require assessment before attributing the presentation to uncomplicated anxiety.
