Reassurance may help but cannot establish stability or the expected course from this uncertain exposure.
Grounding can support comfort while care proceeds but does not replace the needed initial physical and safety assessment.
Prevention teaching is useful after the current condition and disposition needs are understood.
takeaway: Assess acute mental and physical changes after cannabis exposure.
learningObjective: Assess acute mental and physical changes after cannabis exposure.

title: Concurrent mental-health and substance needs
stem: A client receiving care for depression and harmful drinking says each worsens the other. Two services have booked weekly appointments at the same time, and their activity plans conflict. Which plan best addresses the problem?
options: Attend the alcohol service first and revisit mood care later
Attend the mood service first and discuss drinking at future visits
Alternate between services each week using the current plans
With permission, coordinate compatible visits and shared treatment priorities
why: Sequencing alcohol care first may leave the interacting mood problem insufficiently addressed.
Focusing on mood first similarly postpones assessment of drinking that affects symptoms and care.
Alternation may reduce attendance conflict but does not resolve contradictory plans or establish coordinated priorities.
Communication with consent can align feasible care for the interacting concerns rather than leave the client managing conflicting directions.
takeaway: Coordinate care for co-occurring mental-health and substance-use conditions.
learningObjective: Coordinate care for co-occurring mental-health and substance-use conditions.

title: Evaluating recovery support
stem: A client's alcohol-use plan includes two alcohol-free evenings weekly, calling support when cravings escalate and resuming an agreed morning family responsibility. Which follow-up findings show progress toward these goals? Select all that apply.
options: Reports completing two planned alcohol-free evenings this week
Called the chosen support person before acting on an intense craving
A referral to a recovery group was sent by the clinic
Completed the agreed morning responsibility on the planned days
Says they intend to begin changing the routine next month
why: This directly describes completing one agreed behavioural goal.
Actual early help-seeking demonstrates use of the planned response to craving.
A referral is a care-process step but does not establish the client's target outcomes.
Observed or reported completion of the agreed role demonstrates functional progress.
An intention may indicate readiness but is not evidence that the agreed current actions have occurred.
takeaway: Evaluate recovery through agreed goals, functioning and use of support.
learningObjective: Evaluate recovery through agreed goals, functioning and use of support.

title: Gambling-related financial distress
stem: A client describes chasing gambling losses, hiding debt and says, "There is no way out; my family would be better off without me." Which question takes priority?
options: How much money do you currently owe?
Are you thinking about ending your life?
How often have you gambled during the past week?
Who in your family knows about the debt?
why: Debt amount is important to practical support but follows clarification of the self-harm cue.
The hopeless statement warrants direct current suicide inquiry before focusing on financial planning.
Pattern assessment informs treatment but does not establish immediate safety.
Support availability matters, but the client's present intent should be explored directly.
takeaway: Assess safety and functional harm in problematic gambling.
learningObjective: Assess safety and functional harm in problematic gambling.

title: Problematic gaming and function
stem: A student games until 03:00 and repeatedly misses 09:00 classes. They say they can stop whenever they choose. Which question most directly assesses control over the behaviour?
options: How do you usually feel before starting to play?
Do friends play with you during these late sessions?
What happens when you set and try to keep a stopping time?
How many hours do you sleep after the gaming session?
why: Mood may reveal triggers, but does not directly test the claim about ability to stop.
Social context helps understand the activity but does not establish control.
Experience with attempted limits directly explores whether intended stopping translates into action.
Sleep effects demonstrate impact, while the unanswered question concerns ability to limit use.
takeaway: Assess control and functional impairment in potentially addictive behaviours.
learningObjective: Assess control and functional impairment in potentially addictive behaviours.

title: Family boundaries during recovery
stem: A parent has paid an adult child's gambling debts twice and is asked for another loan. The parent wants to remain supportive but protect essential household savings. Which discussion best supports that goal?
options: Explore help with treatment access alongside limits the parent chooses for lending
Work out a smaller new loan that could be repaid over several months
Suggest the parent manage all of the adult child's accounts
Focus on a repayment contract for the next financial request
why: This separates support from repeated lending while leaving financial boundaries with the parent.
A smaller loan may still threaten the savings concern and does not first explore alternatives or limits.
Taking over accounts may be inappropriate and requires consideration of the adult child's autonomy and consent.
A contract may address repayment but does not by itself resolve the pattern or the parent's stated need to protect essential resources.
takeaway: Help families distinguish supportive involvement from taking over consequences.
learningObjective: Help families distinguish supportive involvement from taking over consequences.

title: Choosing peer support
stem: A client wants peer recovery support but found spiritual language in a previous group uncomfortable. They prefer a secular online evening option and have reliable private internet access. What should the nurse offer next?
options: Another meeting of the same group at a different time
A daytime in-person group focused on spiritual recovery
Individual written information to review before seeking peer contact
Information about a secular online evening group and how to try it
why: A time change does not address the stated concern about the format and language.
This conflicts with both the preferred framework and access time.
Written information can help, but does not provide the peer contact the client currently wants.
The option fits the client's stated preferences and practical access, allowing them to evaluate its suitability.
takeaway: Match recovery supports to the client's needs and preferences.
learningObjective: Match recovery supports to the client's needs and preferences.

title: Planning after a substance-related admission
stem: A client is leaving inpatient substance-use treatment for community care. Which findings are unresolved gaps in the transition plan? Select all that apply.
options: The receiving service has not yet confirmed the first appointment
The client does not know whom to contact for urgent recurrence concerns
The chosen support person has agreed to the planned appointment transport
The prescribed treatment will run out before the arranged refill can be obtained
The client can explain the agreed coping action and available crisis number
why: An unconfirmed visit may leave the transition without a usable entry into care.
A clear urgent-response route is needed if problems arise before routine follow-up.
Confirmed feasible transport is a completed support rather than an unresolved gap in this description.
The supply and refill mismatch needs coordinated resolution to avoid interruption.
Demonstrated understanding of the coping and contact plan is a useful completed safeguard.
takeaway: Confirm operational follow-up and treatment continuity after admission.
learningObjective: Confirm operational follow-up and treatment continuity after admission.

title: Strengths in mental-health recovery
stem: A client recovering from mental illness wants to return to gardening. They can remain engaged for about ten minutes before tiring, and a support worker is available. Which first plan best fits the current capacity and goal?
options: Attend the full two-hour community gardening session
Water a few accessible plants with support, then review tolerance
Read a gardening catalogue for the whole activity period
Ask the support worker to complete the garden while the client watches
why: The duration exceeds the currently observed tolerance.
A brief real gardening task with support permits meaningful participation and assessment of a manageable next step.
Planning materials may be interesting but provide less direct participation in the chosen activity.
Observation may help some learning needs, but the client can actively attempt a short task.
takeaway: Organize recovery goals around what the client finds meaningful.
learningObjective: Organize recovery goals around what the client finds meaningful.

title: Supported employment goal
stem: A client returning to work after mental illness asks whether requesting a quieter workspace means they must tell coworkers the diagnosis. What should the nurse do?
options: Help prepare a message announcing the diagnosis to the team
Suggest waiting until coworkers notice a difficulty
Connect the client with appropriate accommodation and disclosure advice
Advise describing the problem as fatigue to avoid questions
why: Broad disclosure should not be assumed to be the client's preferred or necessary route.
Waiting does not help the client make an informed request before a foreseeable barrier arises.
Qualified local advice can clarify options for communicating functional needs and protecting privacy while preserving the client's choices.
A substitute explanation may be inaccurate and does not clarify the actual process or disclosure choices.
takeaway: Support employment goals with individualized practical and privacy advice.
learningObjective: Support employment goals with individualized practical and privacy advice.

title: Self-stigma after diagnosis
stem: A client with depression says, "Having mental illness means I cannot be a good parent." They are worried because low energy has disrupted the child's morning routine. Which reply best supports realistic exploration?
options: Which morning tasks are hardest, and what help or strengths could we build on?
Many parents have depression and still raise children successfully.
You could ask a relative to take over the whole morning routine.
Try to focus on the enjoyable parts of parenting when you feel doubtful.
why: This explores actual function, strengths and support needs without defining parenting ability by the diagnosis.
General reassurance may reduce isolation but does not address the client's concrete concern.
Assistance may be useful, but the scope should reflect assessed needs and preferences rather than immediate full substitution.
Positive experiences matter, but redirecting attention does not examine the disrupted routine.
takeaway: Challenge self-stigma through individualized strengths and functional assessment.
learningObjective: Challenge self-stigma through individualized strengths and functional assessment.

title: Shared decisions in recovery
stem: A stable client says twice-weekly clinic visits threaten a new work schedule and wants the treatment plan reviewed. They want to discuss changes but are unsure how to explain the trade-offs. What is most useful now?
options: Document the concern for the next routine team report
Review why continuing regular attendance has been recommended
Give information about transport to the current appointments
Help prepare goals and burden-related questions for a collaborative review
why: Documentation is necessary but alone may not equip the client to participate in the requested discussion.
Benefits matter, but education should be paired with the client's stated burden and goals.
Transport does not address the conflict with work hours.
Preparing the client's priorities and questions supports informed participation in a review of benefits, burdens and feasible alternatives.
takeaway: Include treatment burden in collaborative recovery planning.
learningObjective: Include treatment burden in collaborative recovery planning.

title: Measuring community recovery
stem: A community mental-health plan aims to maintain the client's tenancy and increase confidence handling housing problems. Which findings demonstrate progress toward those outcomes? Select all that apply.
options: Rent and required housing tasks have been completed for eight weeks
The client used an agreed support contact to resolve a landlord notice
Three housing-resource pamphlets were given at the last visit
The client describes choosing and carrying out the next housing-related step
A referral form was submitted to a community agency
why: Actual maintenance of tenancy responsibilities demonstrates the targeted functional outcome.
Effective use of support in a real problem shows the plan working in the community.
Providing information is a process measure and does not show whether the housing goal was achieved.
Choosing and implementing the next step demonstrates the desired agency and practical confidence.
Referral submission may enable care but is not yet evidence of the client's housing outcome.
takeaway: Evaluate recovery using function, access and client-defined participation.
learningObjective: Evaluate recovery using function, access and client-defined participation.

title: Grief around an anniversary
stem: A client has maintained daily functioning after a partner's death but becomes tearful near the anniversary. Which response best supports the client?
options: What does this anniversary bring up, and what support would feel helpful?
Anniversaries can be difficult; the feelings often become easier with time.
Would keeping busy with a new activity help you avoid a difficult day?
Could you use the same routine you followed on ordinary days last week?
why: Exploring personal meaning and preferred support acknowledges distress without assuming renewed illness or a fixed grief timetable.
Reassurance may normalize the experience but provides less understanding of this client's specific needs.
Activity can help if desired, but assuming avoidance is the goal may not fit the client's wishes.
Routine may be supportive, but should not be assumed to meet the meaning of an anniversary.
takeaway: Explore anniversary-related grief in the context of meaning and function.
learningObjective: Explore anniversary-related grief in the context of meaning and function.

title: Anticipatory grief
stem: A spouse caring for a terminally ill partner says, "I miss the life we shared, even though they are alive." Which reply most directly recognizes the loss being described?
options: The caregiving tasks may be exhausting; tell me which ones are hardest.
You are grieving changes in the shared life you have already lost.
You may be worried about managing alone later; let us discuss that.
You might benefit from a break from care responsibilities this week.
why: Fatigue and burden may coexist, but the statement specifically expresses grief about present losses.
The response recognizes anticipatory grief connected with changes occurring before death.
Future fears may be relevant but differ from the shared life already being missed.
Respite may help burden, but does not directly name the grief expressed.
takeaway: Recognize grief for losses occurring before an anticipated death.
learningObjective: Recognize grief for losses occurring before an anticipated death.

title: Grieving different ways
stem: After a child's death, one parent wants a weekly talking group; the other prefers quiet walks but wants to stay connected with their partner. Both maintain daily function. Which plan best respects both?
options: Arrange weekly group attendance for both parents
Schedule a daily detailed grief discussion as a couple
Support the chosen individual outlets and agree a shared check-in
Replace the different outlets with one joint remembrance activity
why: A shared group may not match the quieter parent's current preference.
A required detailed daily discussion can impose one style of grieving.
Different outlets can meet individual needs while an agreed contact preserves connection.
A remembrance activity may be helpful if chosen, but need not replace preferred individual support.
takeaway: Support different grief expressions without ranking their validity.
learningObjective: Support different grief expressions without ranking their validity.

title: A child asks about death
stem: A five-year-old asks why a deceased grandparent will not wake up. Which explanation is clearest?
options: Grandpa has gone to a peaceful place and will stay there.
Grandpa is resting for a very long time now.
Grandpa was very sick and cannot come home anymore.
Grandpa died; his body stopped working and cannot wake up.
why: This may fit spiritual beliefs but does not explain death clearly and may be interpreted as a reversible journey.
Sleep language can confuse death with ordinary resting and create fear about sleep.
Illness and absence are partial explanations but do not clearly explain the finality of death.
Simple direct wording distinguishes death from sleep; answer further questions honestly at the child's level.
takeaway: Explain death to children using clear developmentally appropriate language.
learningObjective: Explain death to children using clear developmentally appropriate language.

title: Grief requiring further assessment
stem: Which findings in a bereaved client warrant additional clinical assessment? Select all that apply.
options: Persistent inability to meet basic needs
Suicidal thoughts with intent
Occasional tears while discussing memories
Marked sustained functional deterioration
Choosing a culturally meaningful mourning practice
why: Basic self-care failure can create immediate health needs.
Intent requires prompt safety assessment.
Tearfulness alone can occur during adaptive grieving.
Sustained impairment may require additional support or treatment.
Cultural practices should not be pathologized without context.
takeaway: Assess safety and sustained impairment rather than judging grief by tears alone.
learningObjective: Assess safety and sustained impairment rather than judging grief by tears alone.

title: An unrecognized loss
stem: A client grieves a former partner's death and feels isolated because relatives say the relationship should no longer matter. Which response best begins supporting this loss?
options: Could another relative help you find more company this week?
That relationship mattered to you; what are you missing most now?
You might choose a private remembrance activity for the relationship.
Many people grieve former partners, so you are not alone in this feeling.
why: Connection may help, but first acknowledge the particular loss that has been dismissed.
Recognition and an open question validate the relationship's meaning and invite the client's experience.
A remembrance option may be useful after understanding what the client wants.
Normalization can reduce isolation, but offers less exploration of this individual loss than the keyed response.
takeaway: Recognize grief even when others do not validate the relationship or loss.
learningObjective: Recognize grief even when others do not validate the relationship or loss.

title: Offering remembrance choices
stem: After a pregnancy loss, a client is unsure about keepsakes or seeing the infant. What should the nurse do?
options: Describe keepsakes other families valued and encourage the client to select those
Record the current hesitation as a decline and provide the bereavement booklet
Explain the choices, explore concerns and allow the client time to decide
Ask the partner to choose the keepsakes so the client can rest
why: Other families’ experiences may inform discussion but should not prescribe what is meaningful for this client.
Uncertainty calls for information and space; it is not a settled refusal of the available choices.
Sensitive explanation and exploration support an informed personal choice without pressure.
The partner can support the client if desired, but should not replace the client’s preference by default.
takeaway: Offer bereavement choices without assuming what will be meaningful.
learningObjective: Offer bereavement choices without assuming what will be meaningful.

title: Guilt after a death
stem: A client says, 'If I had called sooner, my parent would still be alive.' The cause and preventability are uncertain. What should the nurse say?
options: 'You are carrying a lot of guilt; tell me what you are thinking.'
'Families often wish they had acted differently; try to focus on the good memories.'
'You supported your parent for years; remembering that may help you set this aside.'
'Let us ask for a review of the timeline so we can decide whether the call mattered.'
why: Exploration acknowledges the distress without deciding uncertain causation.
Normalizing can help, but moving directly to positive memories may close discussion of the current guilt.
Past caregiving may be a strength, but advising the client to set guilt aside does not explore its meaning.
A factual discussion may be useful later; immediately making this an investigation bypasses the expressed emotion and cannot promise an answer.
takeaway: Explore bereavement guilt without unsupported promises or judgments.
learningObjective: Explore bereavement guilt without unsupported promises or judgments.

title: Grief and practical needs
stem: A client bereaved last week feels overwhelmed by meals, appointments and paperwork. They have eaten very little today and missed collecting a regular prescription. What should the nurse do first?
options: Offer a bereavement helpline and information about a local support group
Help the client develop a detailed schedule for the next several months
Invite the client to describe memories of the person who died
Identify immediate food and medication needs and available practical help
why: Bereavement services may help, but the unmet needs today require a more immediate practical plan.
A long planning task may add to current overload before basic needs are addressed.
Reminiscence can provide emotional support but does not resolve the stated immediate needs.
Prioritizing basic needs and feasible support makes the next steps manageable.
takeaway: Address practical burdens alongside emotional needs during bereavement.
learningObjective: Address practical burdens alongside emotional needs during bereavement.

title: Supporting a mourning ritual
stem: After a death, a family asks for a bedside mourning ritual the nurse does not know. Some requested timing may conflict with arrangements already planned. Which actions support respectful care? Select all that apply.
options: Ask the family which parts of the ritual are most important to them
Explore feasible changes to the timing with the relevant team
Use the cultural reference guide to select the ritual on the family’s behalf
Explain specific constraints and ask about acceptable alternatives
Arrange the hospital’s usual faith representative to lead the ritual
why: The family’s own account establishes its priorities rather than assuming uniform practice.
Coordination may make the requested practice possible within care arrangements.
A guide can inform respectful questions but cannot establish this family’s choices.
Transparent discussion supports collaboration when the exact request cannot be met.
The usual representative may not fit this family’s beliefs; ask who they would want involved.
takeaway: Ask about mourning practices and collaborate on respectful accommodation.
learningObjective: Ask about mourning practices and collaborate on respectful accommodation.

title: Caregiver overload
stem: A spouse caring for a person with dementia reports sleeping poorly, missing meals and feeling trapped. What should the nurse prioritize?
options: Assess care demands, caregiver wellbeing and immediate options for relief
Review strategies for responding to common dementia behaviours
Help the spouse design a relaxation routine for the evening
Arrange an earlier review of the care recipient’s dementia treatment
why: Missed meals, poor sleep and feeling trapped warrant assessment of caregiver health, safety and practical relief.
Skills education may reduce some demands, but does not by itself establish whether the caregiver’s basic needs and safety are being met.
Relaxation may help sleep but cannot compensate for an unmanageable care workload.
The recipient’s treatment may need review, but the spouse’s own health and support needs also require direct assessment.
takeaway: Assess caregiver health and support before exhaustion becomes a crisis.
learningObjective: Assess caregiver health and support before exhaustion becomes a crisis.

title: Family role changes after illness
stem: A client cannot resume previous household responsibilities after an injury and feels useless. What is the best nursing approach?
options: Focus on regaining the former responsibilities before introducing different household roles
Explore valued roles and agree on achievable contributions with the family
Have relatives take over household planning while physical recovery continues
Set rehabilitation goals around the tasks the family most wants completed
why: Waiting for former roles to return can miss meaningful contributions that are possible now.
Client-valued, achievable participation supports identity and recovery within current limitations.
Temporary help may be needed, but automatically taking over planning can remove an ability the client retains.
Family needs matter, but goals must also reflect the client’s values, abilities and recovery plan.
takeaway: Support meaningful role adaptation after illness or disability.
learningObjective: Support meaningful role adaptation after illness or disability.

title: Adult client and family disagreement
stem: A capable client wants less family involvement in counselling than relatives prefer. What should guide the nurse's plan?
options: Include the main daily caregiver in counselling because they provide most practical support
Begin with a joint family session to resolve the disagreement about participation
Clarify the client’s preferred involvement and agree on what information may be shared
Ask the counsellor to choose participants according to likely treatment benefit
why: Practical support does not replace the capable client’s consent to counselling involvement.
A joint session may be useful if the client agrees, but should not be the default solution to their request for privacy.
Client-defined limits establish legitimate participation and information sharing.
Professional advice can help the client decide, but does not supersede their wishes.
takeaway: Negotiate family involvement with the capable client's consent.
learningObjective: Negotiate family involvement with the capable client's consent.

title: A family requests secrecy
stem: Relatives ask the nurse not to tell a capable adult that a serious diagnosis was confirmed. What is the best next response?
options: Agree to postpone the discussion until relatives feel ready to support it
Arrange a family meeting to decide how much information the client should receive
Ask the clinician to disclose the full diagnosis immediately to ensure openness
Explore family concerns and clarify the client’s information preferences with the team
why: Relatives’ readiness does not establish the capable client’s wishes about receiving information.
Family input may help, but the client should determine their own desired information and involvement.
Honesty matters, but first establish how the client wants information shared, including any wish to involve others or limit detail.
This respects concerns while keeping the capable client’s preferences central to informed communication.
takeaway: Explore family concerns while establishing the client's own information wishes.
learningObjective: Explore family concerns while establishing the client's own information wishes.

title: Family assessment after a crisis
stem: A family is preparing for new daily care responsibilities after a crisis. Which questions directly identify their coping strengths, available support or support gaps? Select all that apply.
options: 'Who could help when meals, appointments or other responsibilities become difficult?'
'What helped your family manage a major change before?'
'How many times has your relative been admitted to hospital this year?'
'What support would make the next few days manageable?'
'What is the current schedule of prescribed medicines?'
why: Potential helpers identify practical and emotional resources.
Previous effective coping can identify strengths to use again.
Admission history describes illness burden; it does not directly establish coping strengths or available help.
The family’s immediate needs identify gaps that support planning can address.
The medicine schedule describes care demands; it does not establish who can manage them or what support is missing.
takeaway: Assess support, previous coping and immediate practical needs in families.
learningObjective: Assess support, previous coping and immediate practical needs in families.

title: Partner violence and readiness
stem: A client discloses partner violence but is not ready to leave. They are currently in a private safe setting. What should the nurse do?
options: Focus the visit on transport and packing for a possible shelter move
Assess current danger and build a safety plan with acceptable resources
Arrange relationship counselling to work on communication with the partner
Provide emergency contact details and invite the client to return when ready
why: Leaving-related preparations may be useful if wanted, but must follow assessment of the client’s current risks, wishes and safe options.
Safety planning can help while the client remains in the relationship; tailor it to current danger and accessible support.
Joint relationship counselling is not an automatic response to coercion or violence and can compromise safety.
Contact information is helpful, but should not replace individualized risk assessment and planning now.
takeaway: Offer safety planning without requiring an immediate decision to leave.
learningObjective: Offer safety planning without requiring an immediate decision to leave.

title: Digital safety after violence
stem: A client experiencing partner violence says their phone is monitored. What should the nurse consider before sending resources?
options: Send a neutral-looking text containing the service telephone number
Email a resource attachment rather than sending a visible text message
Ask which device, contact method and resource format can be used safely
Provide web links and suggest deleting the browser history afterward
why: Even neutral messages can leave records or reveal contact through a monitored device.
Email can also be monitored; changing format does not establish safety.
The client’s knowledge of monitoring should guide a safer communication plan before sending material.
History deletion does not remove every trace and changes may be noticed; assess device safety rather than relying on this step.
takeaway: Check communication safety before sharing violence-related resources.
learningObjective: Check communication safety before sharing violence-related resources.

title: Disclosure of coercive control
stem: A client says a partner controls the money and cancels medical appointments despite the client asking to attend. The client says the partner has never hit them. Which interpretation best guides further assessment?
options: The pattern may be coercive control affecting autonomy and access to care
The pattern primarily reflects an agreed division of household responsibilities
The main difficulty is the client’s lack of knowledge about appointment systems
The absence of physical assault makes ordinary relationship conflict most likely
why: Unwanted control of resources and health-care access can be harmful without physical assault.
The client’s expressed wish to attend is being overridden, so agreement should not be assumed.
The account describes another person blocking access, rather than a stated scheduling-knowledge gap.
No injury does not exclude nonphysical abuse or the need for private safety assessment.
takeaway: Assess controlling behaviours that restrict autonomy and health-care access.
learningObjective: Assess controlling behaviours that restrict autonomy and health-care access.

title: Responding to an assault disclosure
stem: After receiving urgent physical care, an adult survivor says they are unsure about contacting police. What should the nurse do?
options: Encourage a police report promptly so the client will not lose an opportunity to act
Ask whether a relative can help decide before explaining the reporting options
Arrange counselling first and return to discussion of reporting at a later visit
Explain choices and applicable limits, and support the client’s informed decision
why: Time-sensitive evidence options should be explained, but the nurse should not steer a capable adult into a decision without informed discussion.
A chosen supporter may help, but the client needs information and control over whom to involve.
Counselling can be valuable, but postponing information may narrow options the client is currently considering.
Clear options, relevant time considerations and actual reporting limits support agency; requirements depend on the circumstances and jurisdiction.
takeaway: Support informed choices after assault within applicable reporting requirements.
learningObjective: Support informed choices after assault within applicable reporting requirements.

title: Possible financial exploitation
stem: An older adult says a relative uses their bank card and leaves too little money for food. Which actions are appropriate? Select all that apply.
options: Speak privately about the arrangement and the client’s wishes
Assess food access, current safety and the decision-making context
Start with a joint family budget meeting to clarify the spending
Offer appropriate safeguarding and community support options
Provide a household budget worksheet as the initial response to the concern
why: Privacy can help establish consent, control and concerns without another person influencing the account.
Immediate unmet food needs and ability to make decisions may require prompt support.
A joint meeting before private assessment may inhibit disclosure or increase risk when exploitation is possible.
Relevant resources can support safety and informed options while applicable duties are reviewed.
Budget education may be useful for a knowledge gap, but does not first address possible unauthorized control and insufficient food.
takeaway: Assess suspected exploitation privately and address immediate needs.
learningObjective: Assess suspected exploitation privately and address immediate needs.

title: Dementia and distress during bathing
stem: A client with dementia becomes frightened when rushed into a shower but tolerates familiar routines. What should the nurse try?
options: Use a familiar caregiver, slower pacing and one-step explanations
Add a second familiar caregiver so the shower can be completed sooner
Demonstrate the entire shower sequence before beginning the usual routine
Schedule the shower at the usual time and offer a preferred activity afterward
why: The described trigger is rushed care and the client tolerates familiar routines; pacing and familiarity address that pattern.
Additional help may be needed for physical safety, but shortening the task does not necessarily reduce perceived threat from rushing.
A long demonstration may overload processing and leaves pacing during the actual care unchanged.
Consistency and a preferred activity may help, but do not directly address distress caused by how the shower is introduced and paced.
takeaway: Adapt personal care to the person's dementia-related distress cues.
learningObjective: Adapt personal care to the person's dementia-related distress cues.

title: A repeated accusation in dementia
stem: A client with dementia says their purse was stolen; it is safely stored nearby. What is the best response?
options: Remind the client that staff documented where the purse was placed
Acknowledge the worry and help the client find the safely stored purse
Offer a familiar activity to draw attention away from the missing purse
Explain that memory changes can make safely stored belongings seem lost
why: The record may be accurate but does not necessarily reduce the client’s immediate insecurity.
Validation followed by locating the purse addresses the concern and provides concrete reassurance.
Redirection can sometimes help, but an accessible direct resolution is available here.
Education may help at another time, but can be harder to process than finding the item that is causing worry.
takeaway: Respond to the concern beneath dementia-related accusations.
learningObjective: Respond to the concern beneath dementia-related accusations.

title: Sudden withdrawal in dementia
stem: A normally interactive resident with dementia becomes unusually quiet and inattentive over one shift. Which interpretation should guide the nurse’s next assessment?
options: Gradual dementia progression has reduced the resident’s need for interaction
Less agitation indicates that the existing behavioural-care plan is effective
An acute change from baseline may represent hypoactive delirium or illness
Fatigue is the likely explanation because the resident is less physically active
why: A change over one shift is not safely attributed to gradual progression.
Quiet behaviour with new inattention does not establish improvement.
Assess physiology, medicines, pain and other possible contributors and report the acute change; delirium can present with reduced activity.
Fatigue is a possibility, but does not justify overlooking acute cognitive change without assessment.
takeaway: Recognize quiet acute cognitive change as potentially serious.
learningObjective: Recognize quiet acute cognitive change as potentially serious.

title: Pain-related behaviour in dementia
stem: A nonverbal client with dementia grimaces and resists turning after a fall. What should the nurse prioritize?
options: Ask the familiar caregiver to describe behaviour during previous turning care
Use a calm familiar approach and offer a pause before the next turn
Review environmental triggers associated with distress during personal care
Assess for pain and injury using physical and observational findings
why: Baseline behaviour is useful, but the new change after a fall requires direct injury and pain assessment.
Calm pacing supports care, but should accompany rather than replace assessment of the post-fall symptoms.
Environmental triggers may contribute, but a physical injury is a more immediate concern with new guarding and grimacing after a fall.
Nonverbal behaviour may express pain; assess possible injury before treating this simply as care resistance.
takeaway: Assess pain and injury when behaviour changes in a nonverbal client.
learningObjective: Assess pain and injury when behaviour changes in a nonverbal client.

title: Supporting orientation in delirium
stem: Which interventions may support a client with delirium while causes are treated? Select all that apply.
options: Use short calm orientation cues as tolerated
Make needed glasses and hearing aids available
Keep curtains closed throughout the daytime to extend opportunities for sleep
Offer familiar supportive contact suited to the client’s tolerance
Ask the client to repeat orientation answers until each response is accurate
why: Gentle repeated cues can support connection without overwhelming the client.
Sensory access can reduce avoidable misinterpretation and isolation.
Prolonged daytime darkness may disrupt sleep-wake cues rather than restore orientation.
Familiar contact can reduce fear and support communication while causes are treated.
Performance-style repetition can increase fatigue or distress; orientation is supportive care rather than a test the client must pass.
takeaway: Support orientation and sensory access alongside treatment of delirium causes.
learningObjective: Support orientation and sensory access alongside treatment of delirium causes.

title: Wandering with a purpose
stem: A resident with dementia walks toward the exit each afternoon saying they must collect their children. Which information would be most useful for planning an individualized redirection strategy?
options: The resident’s former afternoon routines and the meaning of collecting the children
The resident’s current fall-risk score and usual walking distance
The location of the nearest exit and the daily visitor numbers
The most recent orientation score and errors about the current year
why: The timing and stated purpose can identify a familiar role or unmet need for a meaningful response.
Mobility risk matters for safety, but does not explain why this repeated activity occurs at this time.
Environmental safety matters, but traffic and exit distance do not establish the resident’s underlying concern.
Cognitive testing provides background but does not identify the meaning of this particular pattern.
takeaway: Look for patterns and meaning in dementia-related walking.
learningObjective: Look for patterns and meaning in dementia-related walking.

title: Care choices with cognitive impairment
stem: A client with dementia follows one-step requests and points to preferred clothing, but becomes distressed when the full wardrobe is opened for dressing. Which approach best preserves participation?
options: Lay out several complete outfits so all possibilities are visible together
Offer two suitable garments at a time and allow a simple choice
Use the outfit the client preferred yesterday to shorten the decision
Ask the client to rank clothing preferences on a written list
why: Too many simultaneous options repeat the observed source of overload.
A limited meaningful choice matches the client’s demonstrated ability and preserves current preference.
Past preferences can help, but should not automatically replace a choice the client can still make.
Ranking several written options adds processing demands beyond the one-step ability described.
takeaway: Preserve decision participation appropriate to the person's ability.
learningObjective: Preserve decision participation appropriate to the person's ability.

title: Unexpected touch and aggression
stem: A resident with dementia pushes a caregiver who approaches from behind. What preventive change is most useful?
options: Give the full care explanation from the doorway before approaching the bed
Maintain a running explanation while beginning the hands-on care
Approach within view, identify oneself and explain before each contact
Ask a second caregiver to distract the resident with conversation during care
why: An explanation at a distance may not ensure recognition and readiness when contact occurs.
Narration after touch begins may not prevent the initial surprise that triggered the response.
Visible predictable contact directly addresses startle and perceived threat.
Distraction can help some care, but unexpected touch can remain frightening if approach and preparation are unchanged.
takeaway: Reduce surprise and perceived threat during dementia care.
learningObjective: Reduce surprise and perceived threat during dementia care.

title: Family expects memory recovery
stem: A family repeatedly quizzes a client with dementia and becomes frustrated by incorrect answers. What should the nurse suggest?
options: Use shorter name-and-date quizzes so the client experiences more successful answers
Prepare the correct answers before visits and rehearse them together
Use a family photo album mainly to practise identifying each person
Choose conversation and activities that draw on the client’s remaining interests and abilities
why: Shorter tests can still turn visits into performance demands when repeated quizzing is already distressing.
Rehearsal may not restore lost memory and can displace enjoyable connection.
Photos may support connection, but using them mainly as a naming test can recreate frustration.
Strength-based interaction supports dignity and connection without requiring correct recall.
takeaway: Promote connection rather than repeated memory testing in dementia.
learningObjective: Promote connection rather than repeated memory testing in dementia.

title: Evaluating a behaviour plan
stem: A dementia-care team changes bathing time and uses a familiar caregiver to reduce distress while meeting hygiene needs. Which findings support effectiveness of the revised plan? Select all that apply.
options: Distress episodes during bathing are less frequent and less intense
The client participates in washing with a relaxed expression and fewer pauses
Baths finish faster, but grimacing and attempts to pull away have increased
Skin and hygiene needs are met using the revised approach
The client is quieter after sedating medicine but cannot participate in washing
why: Reduced distress supports the stated aim of the adaptation.
Comfortable participation demonstrates a useful functional response.
Speed does not establish benefit when distress has increased.
The plan must meet necessary physical-care goals as well as reduce distress.
Reduced activity after sedation does not establish comfortable participation or effectiveness of the bathing adaptation.
takeaway: Evaluate dementia adaptations through distress, participation and physical needs.
learningObjective: Evaluate dementia adaptations through distress, participation and physical needs.

title: Delirium education for family
stem: A family says a client's fluctuating confusion means the client is choosing when to cooperate. What should the nurse explain?
options: Attention can fluctuate during delirium even while the underlying illness still needs treatment
The periods of clarity establish that the acute physical problem has resolved
The variation is best understood as steady progression of chronic memory loss
A correct orientation answer shows that difficulties following care instructions have ended
why: Fluctuation is a feature of delirium; repeat assessment and treatment of causes remain necessary.
A lucid interval does not establish recovery of the underlying acute illness.
Rapid fluctuation over hours differs from the usual slower course of chronic cognitive decline.
One correct response does not establish sustained attention or ability to follow a sequence.
takeaway: Explain fluctuating attention without blaming the client.
learningObjective: Explain fluctuating attention without blaming the client.

title: Maintaining identity in dementia
stem: A former gardener with dementia is calmer when tending safe indoor plants. What should the nurse do?
options: Move plant care into the large gardening group to increase social contact
Include the familiar plant-care activity in the individualized daily plan
Rotate several new hobbies each week to broaden cognitive stimulation
Use plant-care sessions to practise recalling plant names and dates
why: Social contact may help, but a larger group has not demonstrated the calming effect of this familiar activity.
The observed response supports retaining a meaningful role and remaining abilities.
Novel activities can be offered, but should not displace a personally meaningful activity that already helps.
Recall exercises may create a performance demand; the demonstrated benefit is meaningful participation rather than testing.
takeaway: Use meaningful familiar activities to support identity in dementia.
learningObjective: Use meaningful familiar activities to support identity in dementia.

title: Medical instability in restrictive eating
stem: An adult receiving care for restrictive eating reports fainting. The pulse is 42/min and blood pressure is 86/52 mmHg. Which action has priority?
options: Obtain a detailed recent intake and compensatory-behaviour history
Explore the fears that have made the current meal plan difficult
Arrange urgent medical assessment for the cardiovascular instability
Review the planned activity level with the eating-disorder team
why: This history is relevant, but must not delay response to fainting with marked bradycardia and hypotension.
Psychological assessment remains important after immediate physical risk is addressed.
Fainting with these observations requires urgent medical assessment and stabilization within coordinated care.
Activity planning matters, but the immediate problem is current physiological instability.
takeaway: Prioritize physical instability in clients with restrictive eating.
learningObjective: Prioritize physical instability in clients with restrictive eating.

title: Weight and eating-disorder risk
stem: A client at an apparently average body size reports frequent vomiting after meals and palpitations. What should the nurse do?
options: Review the measured weight trend and recent changes in intake
Explore situations that trigger vomiting and the associated emotions
Assess the mouth and teeth for longer-term effects of vomiting
Assess current vital signs and escalate possible purging-related cardiac risk
why: Weight and intake contribute to assessment, but apparently average size does not exclude acute complications.
Triggers inform treatment, but palpitations raise a more immediate physical concern.
Dental effects matter, but do not determine current electrolyte or cardiovascular safety.
Frequent vomiting with palpitations warrants prompt physical assessment and clinical escalation for possible complications.
takeaway: Assess eating-disorder behaviour and complications independently of body size.
learningObjective: Assess eating-disorder behaviour and complications independently of body size.

title: Meal support in treatment
stem: A client receiving eating-disorder treatment becomes distressed before a planned meal. Which actions fit a coordinated nursing plan? Select all that apply.
options: Offer calm support using the agreed meal-time coping strategies
Follow the consistent meal-support approach agreed by the team
Offer a lower-energy substitution today to reduce the chance of refusal
Use neutral language about health and coping during the meal
Compare the portion with another client’s to show that it is reasonable
why: Agreed coping support helps the client tolerate distress while remaining engaged.
Consistency supports the coordinated treatment approach.
Unplanned substitutions can reinforce avoidance and should be reviewed through the established plan.
Neutral language supports care without reinforcing appearance-based evaluation.
Comparison may intensify checking or competition rather than address this client’s distress.
takeaway: Provide consistent nonjudgmental meal support within the treatment plan.
learningObjective: Provide consistent nonjudgmental meal support within the treatment plan.

title: Explaining monitoring during nutritional recovery
stem: A client beginning nutritional rehabilitation says, “The blood tests mean the team does not trust me to eat.” The prescribed monitoring has been explained briefly, but the client remains worried. Which response most directly supports understanding and engagement?
options: These checks look for body changes as nutrition restarts; what worries you about them?
Your efforts with meals have been encouraging; let us focus on that progress today.
The checks are part of the usual program; knowing the schedule may make them easier.
The team reviews test results at rounds; would you like the review times written down?
why: This corrects the belief that testing judges cooperation and invites discussion of the client’s concern.
Encouragement may help, but leaves the misunderstanding about monitoring unanswered.
Predictability may reduce anxiety, but describing routine procedure does not explain its clinical purpose.
Access to results matters, but postponing the explanation does not address the present concern about trust.
takeaway: Explain the medical purpose of monitoring while exploring the client’s concerns about treatment.
learningObjective: Explain the medical purpose of monitoring while exploring the client’s concerns about treatment.

title: Body-image statements during care
stem: A client receiving eating-disorder treatment asks, 'Do I look fat now?' What response best supports treatment?
options: Review the recent weight trend to show that recovery is progressing
Explore the anxiety and return to agreed health and coping goals
Reassure the client that their appearance now looks much healthier
Offer another body measurement to settle the immediate uncertainty
why: Clinical weight information may be discussed within the plan, but answering an appearance-checking request this way may miss the underlying anxiety.
Exploring distress supports coping without making external appearance judgment the centre of care.
Well-intended appearance praise can reinforce the importance of body evaluation.
Additional checking for reassurance can maintain the anxiety cycle rather than build coping.
takeaway: Respond to body-image anxiety without reinforcing appearance checking.
learningObjective: Respond to body-image anxiety without reinforcing appearance checking.

title: Binge eating and shame
stem: A client describes episodes of eating with loss of control and intense shame. What is the best nursing response?
options: Start with advice on planning portions and shopping for regular meals
Ask for a calorie diary to guide initial advice about energy intake
Explore the episodes, triggers and distress to guide appropriate support
Begin with a relaxation plan for the periods when eating feels difficult
why: Meal planning may help later, but the loss-of-control pattern and its effects need assessment first.
A calorie-focused record alone does not assess the nature of episodes or distress and may misdirect care.
Nonjudgmental exploration identifies the pattern and needs for coordinated specialist assessment.
Stress strategies can help, but should follow understanding of the episodes rather than replace assessment.
takeaway: Assess loss-of-control eating with a nonjudgmental clinical approach.
learningObjective: Assess loss-of-control eating with a nonjudgmental clinical approach.

title: Exercise despite nutritional instability
stem: A malnourished client continues exercising despite dizziness and a prescribed activity limit. What should the nurse do?
options: Substitute a short slow walk for the workout to maintain participation
Guide paced breathing so the client can finish the current exercise
Review longer-term exercise goals to negotiate a sustainable routine
Pause the activity, assess dizziness and follow the coordinated activity plan
why: Reducing intensity does not establish that exercise is safe during current dizziness and malnutrition.
Breathing support does not address possible physical instability while exercise continues.
Longer-term goals matter after immediate symptoms and current limits are addressed.
Current symptoms require assessment and a safe response consistent with the established care plan.
takeaway: Judge exercise in the context of eating-disorder medical stability.
learningObjective: Judge exercise in the context of eating-disorder medical stability.

title: Eating-disorder recovery outcomes
stem: Which findings support meaningful progress in eating-disorder treatment? Select all that apply.
options: Improved ability to use coping skills around meals
More stable physical status under the treatment plan
Greater focus on comparing body size with others
Improved participation in valued activities
Less disclosure because symptoms feel shameful
why: Coping around meals supports functional recovery.
Physiologic stability is a central treatment outcome.
Increased comparison may reinforce disordered concerns.
Recovery includes life participation beyond food and weight.
Reduced disclosure may conceal worsening symptoms.
takeaway: Evaluate eating-disorder recovery through physical stability, coping and participation.
learningObjective: Evaluate eating-disorder recovery through physical stability, coping and participation.

title: Clarifying figurative instructions
stem: An autistic adult independently follows a written wound-care plan. When told to "keep an eye on it," they ask whether they must look at the wound continuously. The plan specifies one check each morning. Which clarification best addresses the misunderstanding?
options: Look at the wound each morning using the written checklist
Keep watching for changes whenever you are thinking about the wound
The phrase means being alert rather than looking continuously
I can demonstrate how another client checks a similar wound
why: Concrete wording states the intended action and timing in a form that matches the client's demonstrated preference.
This remains vague about when and how often to check.
Defining the phrase partly helps but does not provide the specific action and frequency already in the plan.
Demonstration can help a technique gap, but this client's question concerns the figurative instruction rather than ability to perform care.
takeaway: Clarify figurative language with concrete actions and timing matched to the client's communication needs.
learningObjective: Clarify figurative language with concrete actions and timing matched to the client's communication needs.

title: Communication without spoken language
stem: An autistic adult answers accurately using a familiar communication device and asks to answer the assessment questions themselves. Responses take extra time. Which approach best supports the assessment?
options: Ask the caregiver to summarize answers and invite the client to correct them
Use the client’s established device and allow time for each response
Use nurse-led yes-or-no questions to complete the interview more quickly
Introduce the clinic’s standard picture board for the remaining questions
why: The caregiver may contribute with permission, but leading through them bypasses the client’s stated preference and demonstrated ability.
The familiar system provides effective direct communication and should be accommodated.
A faster restricted format may omit detail the client can express through their own system.
A new board may be useful in some situations, but there is no demonstrated need to replace the effective established method.
takeaway: Preserve access to the client's established communication method.
learningObjective: Preserve access to the client's established communication method.

title: Unexpected routine change
stem: An autistic adolescent becomes overwhelmed when a planned examination order changes. What may help?
options: Describe the equipment in a calm voice before each new examination step
Offer a short break and then resume the examination in the revised order
Review the revised sequence and provide a visual or written plan
Ask the parent to provide reassurance while the changed examination begins
why: Equipment explanations may help, but do not resolve uncertainty about the changed order.
A break can reduce distress, but the client still needs information about what will happen next.
A clear revised sequence restores predictability and supports preparation for the change.
Parent support may be welcome, but beginning without clarifying the change leaves the identified trigger unaddressed.
takeaway: Make changes predictable when routine disruption increases distress.
learningObjective: Make changes predictable when routine disruption increases distress.

title: Pacing teaching around attention recovery
stem: A child with ADHD can correctly practise a complete care sequence while engaged. Attention falls during a long session but returns after a brief movement break. Which plan best uses this observed pattern for the remaining teaching?
options: Move to a quieter area and finish the teaching in one continuous session
Ask the caregiver to take notes during the remaining full explanation
Complete the demonstration first and offer a break afterward
Divide the teaching into shorter blocks with planned movement breaks
why: Less distraction may help, but continuous teaching does not address the observed benefit from interruption and movement.
Notes can support later review but do not restore the child's participation as attention declines.
Delaying the break until all teaching is complete misses the chance to restore engagement during learning.
Planned shorter blocks use the demonstrated recovery after a break while retaining the child's active practice.
takeaway: Match teaching duration and breaks to observed attention and recovery, preserving active participation.
learningObjective: Match teaching duration and breaks to observed attention and recovery, preserving active participation.

title: Escalating sensory overload
stem: Which observations suggest an individualized sensory-support plan needs adjustment? Select all that apply.
options: Distress consistently rises during overlapping staff conversations
The client requests a quieter waiting area
The client uses a familiar communication aid successfully
Care becomes difficult after unexpected physical contact
The client selects a preferred calming activity
why: A repeated trigger identifies an environmental demand to reduce.
A direct request identifies a potentially useful accommodation.
Effective communication access supports rather than undermines the plan.
Unexpected touch can be a modifiable source of overload.
Chosen calming activity can be an effective existing support.
takeaway: Use the client's responses to refine sensory accommodations.
learningObjective: Use the client's responses to refine sensory accommodations.

title: Consistent boundaries across staff
stem: A client asks one nurse to make an exception another nurse declined under the agreed care plan. What should the nurse do?
options: Clarify the current need and respond consistently with the agreed team plan
Allow a one-time exception to preserve rapport during this interaction
Refer the client back to the first nurse to keep the original decision consistent
Restate the existing limit and the next review time before exploring the request
why: The request deserves assessment; new information can be reviewed with the team while maintaining predictable care.
An uncoordinated exception can create confusion without establishing whether the plan needs revision.
Team consistency does not remove the present nurse’s responsibility to hear the client’s concern.
Clear limits help, but the current need should be heard rather than assumed to be unchanged.
takeaway: Combine consistent boundaries with respectful exploration of the need.
learningObjective: Combine consistent boundaries with respectful exploration of the need.

title: Fear of abandonment after a schedule change
stem: A client says a nurse's planned absence proves nobody cares. What is the most therapeutic response?
options: Explain that the covering nurses have the same training and experience
Acknowledge the feeling and explain who will provide care during the absence
Offer to postpone the next conversation until the usual nurse returns
Review the coping skills that helped during earlier difficult separations
why: Competence reassurance may help, but does not fully acknowledge the distress or make the continuity plan concrete.
Validation plus an understandable coverage plan addresses the fear without unrealistic promises.
Postponement may reinforce dependence and leaves current support uncertain.
Coping skills can complement the response, but should not replace clarifying reliable ongoing care.
takeaway: Address abandonment fears with validation and predictable continuity.
learningObjective: Address abandonment fears with validation and predictable continuity.

title: Requests for personal social contact
stem: A client nearing discharge asks to connect with the nurse's personal social-media account. What should the nurse do?
options: Accept the request with access limited to viewing rather than messaging
Create a separate personal account for clients after they leave the service
Explain the boundary and review appropriate ongoing support contacts
Ask the client to send the request again after discharge is complete
why: Restricted visibility does not turn a personal social-media relationship into an appropriate professional care channel.
A personal account for former clients still creates boundary and confidentiality concerns outside approved systems.
A respectful explanation and appropriate support contacts maintain boundaries and continuity.
Completion of discharge does not automatically make personal social-media contact appropriate.
takeaway: Redirect personal-contact requests toward appropriate continuing supports.
learningObjective: Redirect personal-contact requests toward appropriate continuing supports.

title: Anger after a limit
stem: A client raises their voice when a previously agreed boundary is maintained. No immediate physical threat is present. What should the nurse do?
options: Explain the full policy in detail so the client understands why the limit exists
Offer a one-time exception to settle the situation and discuss the limit later
Invite negotiation of a new limit while the client is most upset
Acknowledge frustration and restate the limit with a feasible alternative
why: Detailed reasoning during heightened emotion may overwhelm rather than help regulation; a concise explanation is more useful.
An exception made to end distress can undermine the agreed plan without assessing a clinical reason to change it.
Complex negotiation during peak distress is less useful than calm clarity; review can occur when the client can engage.
Validation, a clear consistent limit and an acceptable option support regulation and predictable care.
takeaway: Maintain boundaries calmly while offering acceptable alternatives.
learningObjective: Maintain boundaries calmly while offering acceptable alternatives.

title: Reflecting on strong reactions
stem: A nurse feels unusually irritated by a client's repeated requests. Which actions support therapeutic care? Select all that apply.
options: Reflect on personal reactions and possible bias
Seek appropriate supervision or team consultation
Set a stricter request-frequency rule for clients who present this pattern
Continue objective assessment of the client’s current needs
Explain personal frustration in detail to encourage mutual understanding
why: Reflection helps prevent the nurse’s emotional reaction from determining care.
Consultation can help identify a consistent response and support the nurse.
A blanket restriction based on irritation can miss individual needs and requires proper assessment and team review.
Observable needs and behaviour should continue to guide care.
Detailed disclosure of the nurse’s frustration can shift emotional responsibility to the client rather than support therapeutic assessment.
takeaway: Use reflection and consultation when personal reactions affect care.
learningObjective: Use reflection and consultation when personal reactions affect care.

title: Spiritual distress after diagnosis
stem: A client says, 'My illness means I am being punished.' What should the nurse do?
options: Explore what punishment means to the client and ask what support would help
Explain the biological cause of the illness to reassure the client
Redirect the discussion toward the positive possibilities of treatment
Contact the faith representative listed in the chart to provide reassurance
why: Open exploration assesses spiritual distress and the client’s preferred support without imposing an interpretation.
Biological information may help, but does not necessarily address the personal meaning or distress.
Hope is valuable, but redirection can leave the expressed concern unheard.
Previous affiliation does not establish the client’s current wishes for spiritual support or information sharing.
takeaway: Explore spiritual distress without imposing or confirming an explanation.
learningObjective: Explore spiritual distress without imposing or confirming an explanation.

title: A request for prayer
stem: A client asks for spiritual support before a difficult procedure. The nurse does not share the belief. What is the best response?
options: Suggest waiting for family to lead prayer after the procedure
Ask what support is desired and facilitate an appropriate resource
Offer a relaxation exercise in place of the requested spiritual support
Select a prayer recording using the religious affiliation in the chart
why: Family support may be welcome, but waiting may not address the present request before the procedure.
Client-defined assistance supports spiritual needs without requiring the nurse to share the belief.
Relaxation can complement care but should not automatically replace the requested form of support.
Recorded affiliation alone does not establish the client’s preferred practice; ask before selecting support.
takeaway: Facilitate spiritual support according to the client's wishes.
learningObjective: Facilitate spiritual support according to the client's wishes.

title: Caregiver guilt about respite
stem: A caregiver says, 'Accepting respite means I have failed my parent.' What response best supports reflection?
options: Describe the health benefits of respite and provide a list of services
Reassure the caregiver that many devoted relatives use respite successfully
Explore what good caregiving means and how rest can support continued care
Start arranging available respite dates to make accepting help easier
why: Information may be useful, but does not directly explore the belief that rest represents failure.
Normalization can help, but may leave the caregiver’s personal meaning and guilt unexplored.
Exploring values can help the caregiver connect sustainable support with continued caring.
Practical arrangements should follow understanding of the concern and the caregiver’s choices.
takeaway: Explore caregiving values when guilt prevents needed support.
learningObjective: Explore caregiving values when guilt prevents needed support.

title: Evaluating crisis resolution
stem: After an acute situational crisis, a client appears calmer but still cannot identify a safe place to stay tonight. What should the nurse prioritize?
options: Review the coping strategies that reduced distress during the interview
Arrange a referral for longer-term counselling about the precipitating event
Repeat the distress rating to confirm that the apparent improvement persists
Confirm a safe place tonight and the practical arrangements for follow-up
why: Coping is important, but improvement does not resolve the stated lack of safe accommodation.
Longer-term treatment can follow, but does not secure tonight’s immediate needs.
Symptom reassessment is useful, but a lower distress score cannot establish a safe discharge plan.
An actionable accommodation and follow-up plan addresses the unresolved practical risk.
takeaway: Evaluate crisis recovery through practical safety and coping, not appearance alone.
learningObjective: Evaluate crisis recovery through practical safety and coping, not appearance alone.

title: A client-defined support network
stem: A client preparing for discharge names a close friend who has agreed to provide transport to appointments. Other support needs remain. Which nursing actions help create a workable support plan? Select all that apply.
options: Ask whom else the client considers supportive and wants involved
Confirm the transport arrangements and what the friend can realistically provide
Record the friend as available for overnight help because the relationship is close
Discuss professional or community resources for remaining support needs
Send the full care summary to the friend based on the transport agreement
why: The client defines the support network and who may be involved.
Clarifying specific availability and tasks makes the plan practical.
Closeness and a transport agreement do not establish willingness or availability for overnight care.
Formal resources can address needs beyond the agreed informal help.
Agreement to provide transport does not by itself authorize sharing the full care summary.
takeaway: Build support plans from the client's relationships, consent and realistic resources.
learningObjective: Build support plans from the client's relationships, consent and realistic resources.

title: Relocation and continuity of identity
stem: An older adult newly admitted to assisted living withdraws from meals and says nothing feels familiar. No acute illness is identified. What should the nurse do?
options: Repeat the facility orientation tour and review the printed activity timetable
Explore familiar routines and meaningful belongings that could support adjustment
Arrange a place at a communal meal table with regular organized activities
Provide meals in the room for a week so the client can settle in quietly
why: Orientation information may help, but does not establish which personal routines or connections the client is missing.
Exploring what is familiar and meaningful supports an individualized transition plan.
Social opportunities may help when matched to preferences; arranging them first may miss the source of withdrawal.
A quieter setting may be appropriate by preference, but automatically withdrawing communal opportunities can increase isolation.
takeaway: Preserve familiar routines and identity during a major living transition.
learningObjective: Preserve familiar routines and identity during a major living transition.
